questions.question: What is a Java annotation?

options.text: Metadata attached to program elements that can be processed by the compiler, tools, or at runtime.
A special kind of thread used by the JVM.
A replacement for an interface.
A command that executes SQL at compile time.

questions.explanation: Annotations provide metadata on declarations such as classes, methods, fields, parameters, and types. They can be consumed by the compiler, build tools, annotation processors, or runtime frameworks through reflection, depending on their retention policy.

questions.question: What is the difference between `SOURCE`, `CLASS`, and `RUNTIME` annotation retention?

options.text: SOURCE is retained in source only; CLASS is recorded in class files but not required at runtime; RUNTIME is available through runtime reflection.
SOURCE is available at runtime; CLASS is source-only; RUNTIME is removed by the compiler.
All three have identical behavior.
RUNTIME annotations are available only to the Java compiler.

questions.explanation: `RetentionPolicy.SOURCE` annotations are discarded by the compiler. `CLASS` annotations are recorded in the class file but need not be available through reflection. `RUNTIME` annotations are retained for runtime reflective access.

questions.question: What does `@Target` specify in a custom annotation?

options.text: The Java version required by the annotation.
The program element locations where the annotation is permitted, such as TYPE, METHOD, FIELD, or PARAMETER.
The runtime class loader that creates the annotation.
The order in which annotation methods execute.

questions.explanation: `@Target` restricts where an annotation may be applied. Its ElementType values include TYPE, FIELD, METHOD, PARAMETER, CONSTRUCTOR, LOCAL_VARIABLE, ANNOTATION_TYPE, PACKAGE, TYPE_USE, and others. If omitted, the annotation can be applied broadly to declaration contexts.

questions.question: What is reflection in Java?

options.text: The ability to inspect and, where permitted, interact with class metadata and members at runtime.
A compiler optimization that removes unused methods.
A way to execute code on a second CPU core.
A mechanism for automatically generating database indexes.

questions.explanation: Reflection APIs such as Class, Field, Method, and Constructor allow runtime inspection of types and members, and can invoke methods or access fields subject to access checks and module boundaries. Frameworks use reflection for dependency injection, serialization, and mapping.

questions.question: How can you obtain a `Class<?>` object for a Java type?

options.text: Only by constructing an instance and calling `toString()`.
Using `SomeType.class`, `object.getClass()`, or `Class.forName()` for a class name.
Only through the garbage collector.
By calling `new Class()`.

questions.explanation: A class literal such as `String.class` obtains the Class object without an instance. `obj.getClass()` returns the runtime class of an object. `Class.forName("fully.qualified.Name")` loads and initializes a class by name under its documented semantics.

questions.question: What is an annotation processor?

options.text: A runtime thread that executes every annotation method.
A compile-time tool that processes annotations and can validate code or generate source files and other artifacts.
A garbage collector specialized for annotated classes.
A JDBC driver feature.

questions.explanation: Annotation processors use the language-model and processing APIs (javax.annotation.processing in the Java platform) to inspect annotations during compilation. They can issue diagnostics and generate source or resource files. Examples include processors used by code-generation libraries.

questions.question: What is a dynamic proxy in Java?

options.text: An object generated at runtime that implements specified interfaces and delegates method calls to an InvocationHandler.
A proxy server that routes HTTP requests outside the JVM.
A subclass that can override any final class method.
A database connection pool.

questions.explanation: `java.lang.reflect.Proxy` can create a runtime proxy implementing one or more interfaces. Calls are dispatched to an InvocationHandler. Dynamic proxies are useful for cross-cutting behavior such as logging or transaction interception, but the standard proxy mechanism is interface-based.

questions.question: What limitation should you remember when using Java reflection to access private members?

options.text: Reflection always bypasses all access controls in every module.
Access can be restricted by Java access checks and module boundaries; deep reflection may require packages to be opened.
Private members are never represented in reflection metadata.
Reflection can access fields but cannot inspect methods.

questions.explanation: Reflection does not guarantee unrestricted access. Java language access checks and the module system can prevent deep reflective access to non-public members in another module unless the package is appropriately opened. Avoid depending on private implementation details where possible.

questions.question: What is the Java Collections Framework hierarchy?

options.text: Collection → List, Set, Queue; Map is separate (not a Collection)
Collection → List, Set, Map, Queue (all inherit from Collection)
Array → Collection → List, Set, Map
Object → Collection → List → ArrayList, LinkedList, HashMap

questions.explanation: The root interface is `Collection<E>` with subinterfaces: `List` (ordered, duplicates allowed), `Set` (no duplicates), `Queue`/`Deque` (FIFO/LIFO). `Map<K,V>` is a separate hierarchy — it does NOT extend Collection. Common: ArrayList, LinkedList (List); HashSet, TreeSet (Set); HashMap, TreeMap (Map); ArrayDeque (Queue/Deque).

questions.question: What is the difference between `ArrayList` and `LinkedList`?

options.text: ArrayList: O(1) random access, O(n) insert/delete at middle; LinkedList: O(n) random access, O(1) insert/delete at known node
ArrayList is thread-safe; LinkedList is not
LinkedList uses less memory than ArrayList
ArrayList allows null; LinkedList does not

questions.explanation: ArrayList: backed by an array, O(1) get(index), O(n) add/remove in the middle (shifts elements), amortized O(1) add at end, better cache locality. LinkedList: doubly-linked nodes, O(1) add/remove at head/tail if you have the node reference, O(n) get(index). In practice, ArrayList outperforms LinkedList for most workloads due to cache efficiency — prefer ArrayList unless you specifically need O(1) head/tail operations.

questions.question: What is the difference between `HashMap`, `LinkedHashMap`, and `TreeMap`?

options.text: HashMap: O(1) get/put, no order; LinkedHashMap: insertion-order or access-order; TreeMap: sorted by key, O(log n) operations
HashMap is synchronized; LinkedHashMap is not; TreeMap is read-only
TreeMap is fastest; HashMap is slowest
They are identical — just different naming conventions

questions.explanation: HashMap: hash table, O(1) average get/put, no guaranteed order, allows one null key. LinkedHashMap: extends HashMap, maintains insertion order (or access order for LRU cache). TreeMap: Red-Black tree, keys sorted by natural order or Comparator, O(log n) for all operations — useful for range queries (`subMap`, `headMap`, `tailMap`).

questions.question: How does HashMap work internally?

options.text: HashMap stores key-value pairs in a sorted array
HashMap uses an array of buckets; keys are hashed to a bucket index, stored in a linked list (or tree for large buckets) within that bucket
HashMap stores entries in a balanced binary search tree
HashMap uses a matrix of (key, value) pairs indexed by both dimensions

questions.explanation: HashMap maintains an array (default 16 slots). To put a key: compute `hashCode()`, apply bit manipulation for index, store in that bucket. Collisions: Java 7 uses linked list per bucket; Java 8+ converts to TreeMap (red-black tree) when bucket has ≥ 8 entries (treeification). Load factor (default 0.75): when 75% full, the backing array doubles (rehashing). O(1) average; O(n) worst case with bad hash function.

questions.question: What is the difference between `HashSet` and `TreeSet`?

options.text: HashSet: O(1) operations, no order; TreeSet: O(log n) operations, elements sorted by natural/Comparator order
HashSet allows duplicates; TreeSet does not
TreeSet is faster than HashSet for all operations
HashSet is thread-safe; TreeSet is not

questions.explanation: HashSet: backed by HashMap (element is key, dummy value), O(1) add/contains/remove, no guaranteed iteration order. TreeSet: backed by TreeMap (NavigableSet), O(log n) all operations, elements always sorted. Use HashSet for fast membership checks; use TreeSet when you need sorted order or range operations (`headSet`, `tailSet`, `subSet`, `floor`, `ceiling`).

questions.question: What is the difference between `Comparable` and `Comparator`?

options.text: Comparable defines the natural ordering within the class itself; Comparator is an external strategy for comparing two objects
Comparable is for sorting collections; Comparator is for sorting arrays
Comparator is built into the class; Comparable is external
They are identical — use whichever you prefer

questions.explanation: `Comparable<T>` is implemented by the class to define its natural order: `compareTo(T other)`. `Comparator<T>` is a separate object providing an alternative or external comparison: `compare(T a, T b)`. Use Comparable when there is one obvious sort order; use Comparator for multiple orderings or when you can't modify the class. `Collections.sort(list, comparator)` and `list.sort(comparator)`.

questions.question: What is `ConcurrentModificationException` and how do you avoid it?

options.text: An exception that occurs when two threads modify the same object
Thrown when a collection is structurally modified while iterating over it with an Iterator — avoid by using Iterator.remove(), CopyOnWriteArrayList, or collecting changes and applying after iteration
An exception thrown when a collection runs out of memory
Thrown only in multithreaded code when two threads access the same list

questions.explanation: Most Java collections use a `modCount` counter. Iterators capture the count on creation and check it on each `next()` call — if modified externally, it throws ConcurrentModificationException (fail-fast). Solutions: (1) `iterator.remove()` — safe removal during iteration. (2) `removeIf(predicate)` on the collection. (3) Collect elements to remove, then removeAll after. (4) Use `CopyOnWriteArrayList` for concurrent use.

questions.question: What is `Collections.unmodifiableList()` vs `List.of()` vs `List.copyOf()`?

options.text: They are identical — all create immutable lists
`unmodifiableList()`: a view that prevents modification but the backing list can change; `List.of()`: truly immutable, no nulls; `List.copyOf()`: immutable defensive copy of an existing collection
`List.of()` allows nulls; the others do not
`Collections.unmodifiableList()` is the modern replacement for `List.of()`

questions.explanation: `Collections.unmodifiableList(list)` wraps a mutable list — the wrapper throws on mutation calls, but if the underlying list is modified directly, the view reflects that change. `List.of(1,2,3)` (Java 9): truly immutable, no nulls, fixed size. `List.copyOf(collection)` (Java 10): creates an immutable snapshot. For truly immutable collections, prefer `List.of()` or `List.copyOf()`.

questions.question: When would you choose a `Deque` over a `Queue`?

options.text: When you need to add/remove from both ends (double-ended queue) — use ArrayDeque as a stack (push/pop) or queue (offer/poll)
Use Deque when the queue must be synchronized
Deque is only for LIFO; Queue is only for FIFO
Deque is slower than Queue — only use it for large datasets

questions.explanation: `Deque` (double-ended queue) supports insertion/removal at both front and back. `ArrayDeque` is the most efficient general-purpose implementation — faster than `LinkedList` for both stack and queue use cases. Java docs recommend `ArrayDeque` over `Stack` (which is synchronized and extends Vector). Use `offerFirst`/`pollFirst` (stack) or `offerLast`/`pollFirst` (queue).

questions.question: What is `PriorityQueue` and what ordering does it use?

options.text: PriorityQueue is a FIFO queue with automatic alphabetical ordering
PriorityQueue is a min-heap — the smallest element (by natural order or Comparator) is always at the head
PriorityQueue maintains insertion order with a priority number
PriorityQueue is a synchronized version of ArrayDeque

questions.explanation: PriorityQueue is a heap-based priority queue. `poll()` always returns the smallest element (min-heap). For max-heap: `new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder())`. O(log n) for offer/poll, O(1) for peek. Not thread-safe. Iteration order is undefined — only `poll()` guarantees priority order. Used for Dijkstra, task scheduling, top-K problems.

questions.question: What is the initial capacity and load factor of HashMap, and how do they affect performance?

options.text: Initial capacity: 10, load factor: 0.5 — these cannot be changed

Initial capacity: 16, load factor: 0.75. When entries exceed capacity×loadFactor, the map rehashes (doubles capacity). Lower load factor = fewer collisions, more memory; higher = more collisions, less memory
Initial capacity: 100, load factor: 1.0 — the default is optimized for all cases
Initial capacity and load factor only matter for LinkedHashMap

questions.explanation: Default: 16 buckets, 0.75 load factor. Rehash when size > 16×0.75=12. Rehashing doubles the array and re-distributes all entries — O(n) operation. If you know the final size, pre-size: `new HashMap<>(expectedSize / 0.75 + 1)` to avoid rehashing. Lower load factor (e.g. 0.5) reduces collisions at cost of more memory; higher (e.g. 0.9) saves memory but increases collision rate.

questions.question: What is `EnumMap` and `EnumSet` and when should you use them?

options.text: EnumMap and EnumSet are deprecated — use HashMap and HashSet instead

EnumMap: a Map implementation optimized for enum keys using an array (O(1), compact); EnumSet: a Set implementation for enum values using bit manipulation — both are faster than their general-purpose equivalents when keys are enums
EnumMap sorts entries by enum ordinal; EnumSet maintains insertion order
They are identical to HashMap/HashSet but restricted to String keys

questions.explanation: EnumMap uses an array indexed by `enum.ordinal()` — O(1) and extremely compact, no hashing overhead. EnumSet uses a bit vector (single `long` for enums with ≤64 constants) — blazing fast, no boxing. Both maintain declaration order. Always use these when your key/element type is an enum — significant performance and memory advantage.

questions.question: What is the difference between `Vector` and `ArrayList`, and should you use `Vector`?

options.text: Vector is the modern replacement for ArrayList
Vector is a legacy synchronized list (all methods synchronized) — use ArrayList for single-threaded code; use CopyOnWriteArrayList or synchronized wrappers for thread-safety instead
Vector is faster than ArrayList because it pre-allocates more memory
ArrayList is deprecated; Vector is the current standard

questions.explanation: Vector predates the Collections Framework (Java 1.0). It synchronizes every method, causing unnecessary overhead in single-threaded code. ArrayList (Java 1.2) replaced it. For thread-safe lists: `Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>())` or `CopyOnWriteArrayList`. `Stack` (extends Vector) should be replaced with `ArrayDeque`. Don't use Vector in new code.

questions.question: What is `WeakHashMap` and when would you use it?

options.text: WeakHashMap is a HashMap that allows null values
WeakHashMap holds weak references to keys — when a key is no longer referenced elsewhere, it is eligible for garbage collection and the entry is removed automatically
WeakHashMap is a slower HashMap used for testing purposes
WeakHashMap requires keys to implement WeakReference interface

questions.explanation: WeakHashMap's keys are held via WeakReferences. When a key has no other strong references, the GC can reclaim it — the WeakHashMap entry is then removed. Use cases: caches where entries should be collected when the cached object is no longer used elsewhere (e.g. per-Class metadata, listener registries). Not thread-safe. Contrast with regular HashMap which prevents GC of its keys.

questions.question: How do you correctly remove elements from a List while iterating?

options.text: Use a for-each loop and call list.remove(element) inside
Use Iterator and call iterator.remove(), or use list.removeIf(predicate), or iterate backwards with a traditional for loop
Use a for loop with an index and never skip indices
Collections cannot be modified during iteration — create a new list instead

questions.explanation: For-each with `list.remove()` throws ConcurrentModificationException. Safe approaches: (1) `Iterator<E> it = list.iterator(); while(it.hasNext()) { if(condition) it.remove(); }` (2) `list.removeIf(e -> condition)` — cleanest. (3) Traditional for loop iterating backwards: `for(int i=list.size()-1; i>=0; i--) { if(condition) list.remove(i); }` — safe because removals don't affect unvisited indices.

questions.question: What is `Map.getOrDefault()`, `Map.computeIfAbsent()`, and `Map.merge()` used for?

options.text: They are deprecated — use get() and put() for all Map operations
getOrDefault: get with fallback; computeIfAbsent: lazy compute and cache; merge: combine existing value with new value — all reduce boilerplate for common Map patterns
They are used only with ConcurrentHashMap
computeIfAbsent and merge only work with Integer values

questions.explanation: `getOrDefault(key, default)`: returns value or default without null-check. `computeIfAbsent(key, k -> value)`: if key absent, computes and puts value — perfect for `Map<String, List<>>` grouping. `merge(key, value, (old,new) -> combined)`: if key absent puts value; if present applies merge function — perfect for frequency counting: `map.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum)`.

questions.question: What is the difference between `Arrays.asList()` and `List.of()`?

options.text: They are identical — both return an immutable fixed-size list
`Arrays.asList()`: fixed-size but mutable (set() works, add/remove throw); backed by the array — changes to the array reflect in the list. `List.of()`: fully immutable, no nulls allowed
`List.of()` is backed by an array; `Arrays.asList()` is backed by a LinkedList
`Arrays.asList()` is deprecated; use `List.of()` for all cases

questions.explanation: `Arrays.asList(arr)` returns a fixed-size List backed by the original array — `set()` works and changes are reflected in the array, but `add()`/`remove()` throw UnsupportedOperationException. Allows null. `List.of(1,2,3)` (Java 9): fully immutable — set/add/remove all throw, null elements throw NullPointerException. Choose `List.of()` for truly immutable collections.

questions.question: What is `IdentityHashMap` and when would you use it?

options.text: IdentityHashMap uses == for key comparison instead of equals()
IdentityHashMap is a HashMap where keys must implement an Identity interface
IdentityHashMap is a WeakHashMap with identity-based comparison
IdentityHashMap requires keys to be Strings

questions.explanation: `IdentityHashMap` uses reference equality (`==`) and `System.identityHashCode()` for keys instead of `equals()`/`hashCode()`. Two distinct objects with equal content are treated as different keys. Use cases: object graph serialization (tracking visited objects to detect cycles), proxy caches keyed by identity, compiler symbol tables.

questions.question: What is `Collections.sort()` vs `List.sort()` vs `Arrays.sort()`?

options.text: Collections.sort() is for arrays; Arrays.sort() is for lists

Collections.sort(list): sorts a List, delegates to list.sort() since Java 8. List.sort(comparator): instance method. Arrays.sort(array): sorts primitive arrays (dual-pivot quicksort) or Object arrays (Timsort). All are O(n log n).
Arrays.sort() is slower — always prefer Collections.sort()
They use different algorithms and cannot be used interchangeably

questions.explanation: `Collections.sort(list)` and `list.sort(null)` are equivalent since Java 8 — both use Timsort (O(n log n), stable). `Arrays.sort(int[])` uses dual-pivot quicksort (not stable, faster for primitives). `Arrays.sort(Object[])` uses Timsort (stable). For parallel sorting of large arrays: `Arrays.parallelSort()` uses fork/join. Prefer `list.sort(comparator)` for readability.

questions.question: What is `ConcurrentHashMap` and how does it differ from `Collections.synchronizedMap()`?

options.text: They are identical — both lock the entire map on every operation

ConcurrentHashMap uses segment/bucket-level locking (allows concurrent reads and some concurrent writes); synchronizedMap locks the entire map for every operation — ConcurrentHashMap is much more performant under concurrent access
synchronizedMap is more modern; ConcurrentHashMap is legacy
ConcurrentHashMap does not support null keys; synchronizedMap does

questions.explanation: `synchronizedMap` wraps a map with a single mutex — every read and write is serialized. `ConcurrentHashMap` (Java 5+): reads are lock-free; writes use bucket-level CAS/synchronized (Java 8: node-level locking), enabling true concurrent reads and high write concurrency. Also supports atomic operations: `putIfAbsent`, `computeIfAbsent`, `merge`. Does not allow null keys or values.

questions.question: What is the difference between `Iterator` and `ListIterator`?

options.text: Iterator is for forward-only traversal; ListIterator is for Lists only and supports bidirectional traversal, modification, and index access
ListIterator is the old API; Iterator is the modern replacement
Iterator supports modification; ListIterator is read-only
They are identical — ListIterator just has a longer name

questions.explanation: `Iterator`: forward-only, works on any Iterable (`hasNext()`, `next()`, `remove()`). `ListIterator` (extends Iterator): works only on Lists, supports bidirectional traversal (`hasPrevious()`, `previous()`), modification (`set()`, `add()`), and index queries (`nextIndex()`, `previousIndex()`). Use `list.listIterator()` to get one.

questions.question: What does `Collections.frequency()`, `Collections.disjoint()`, and `Collections.nCopies()` do?

options.text: These methods do not exist in the Collections class
`frequency(collection, obj)`: count occurrences; `disjoint(c1, c2)`: true if no common elements; `nCopies(n, obj)`: immutable list of n copies of obj
`frequency()` returns the most frequent element; `disjoint()` returns duplicate-free version; `nCopies()` creates a synchronized list
They are only available in Java 11+

questions.explanation: Useful utility methods: `Collections.frequency(list, "a")` — counts how many times "a" appears. `Collections.disjoint(set1, set2)` — true if they share no elements (intersection is empty). `Collections.nCopies(3, "x")` — returns `["x", "x", "x"]` as an immutable list, useful for initializing or filling collections.

questions.question: What is `NavigableMap` and what operations does it add over `SortedMap`?

options.text: NavigableMap is just a renamed SortedMap — they have the same methods
NavigableMap extends SortedMap with navigation methods: floor, ceiling, lower, higher, pollFirstEntry, pollLastEntry, and descendingMap
NavigableMap is a concurrent version of SortedMap
NavigableMap supports range queries; SortedMap does not

questions.explanation: `SortedMap` provides `firstKey()`, `lastKey()`, `headMap()`, `tailMap()`, `subMap()`. `NavigableMap` (extends SortedMap, implemented by TreeMap) adds: `floor(k)` (greatest key ≤ k), `ceiling(k)` (least key ≥ k), `lower(k)` (strictly <), `higher(k)` (strictly >), `pollFirstEntry()`, `pollLastEntry()`, `descendingMap()`. Very useful for interval lookups and ordered event processing.

questions.question: What is `ArrayDeque` and why is it preferred over `Stack` and `LinkedList` as a stack/queue?

options.text: ArrayDeque is slower — use Stack for stacks and LinkedList for queues
ArrayDeque uses a resizable array with no per-element overhead — faster than LinkedList (cache locality) and unsynchronized unlike Stack
ArrayDeque is synchronized; Stack and LinkedList are not
ArrayDeque only supports FIFO; it cannot be used as a stack

questions.explanation: `Stack` is synchronized (unnecessary overhead) and extends `Vector` (legacy). `LinkedList` has per-node memory overhead and poor cache performance. `ArrayDeque` (circular buffer backed by array): no synchronization overhead, excellent cache locality, amortized O(1) for all deque operations. Java docs explicitly recommend `ArrayDeque` over `Stack`. Use `push`/`pop` for stack semantics, `offer`/`poll` for queue.

questions.question: How would you find the duplicate elements in a List efficiently?

options.text: Sort the list and check adjacent elements — O(n log n)
Use a HashSet: iterate the list, add each element to the set — elements that return false from add() are duplicates. O(n) time, O(n) space
Compare every element to every other element — O(n²)
Use Collections.frequency() for each element — O(n²)

questions.explanation: Optimal approach: `Set<T> seen = new HashSet<>(); Set<T> dups = new HashSet<>(); for(T e : list) { if(!seen.add(e)) dups.add(e); }` — O(n) time, O(n) space. `Set.add()` returns false if the element was already present. Alternatively: `list.stream().filter(e -> Collections.frequency(list, e) > 1).collect(toSet())` — simpler but O(n²).

questions.question: What is the difference between `List`, `Set`, and `Map`?

options.text: List is ordered and permits duplicates; Set enforces uniqueness; Map stores key-value associations
List stores key-value pairs; Set preserves duplicates; Map is always sorted
All three interfaces guarantee insertion order
Set and Map both extend List

questions.explanation: List represents an ordered sequence and permits duplicate elements. Set models uniqueness and does not permit duplicate elements according to its equality/ordering rules. Map associates keys with values and requires unique keys; Map is not a subtype of Collection.

questions.question: What happens if two different keys in a HashMap have the same hash code?

options.text: The second entry always overwrites the first
The map throws an exception
The keys share a bucket, and HashMap uses equality checks to distinguish them
HashMap converts both keys into one key

questions.explanation: A hash collision occurs when different keys map to the same bucket. HashMap stores both entries and uses equals() to determine whether a key already exists. A correct key implementation must obey the equals() and hashCode() contract. In modern Java, heavily populated buckets may be treeified under implementation-specific thresholds.

questions.question: What is the difference between fail-fast and weakly consistent iterators?

options.text: Fail-fast iterators always work on immutable snapshots
Weakly consistent iterators may reflect some concurrent updates without throwing ConcurrentModificationException; fail-fast iterators may throw when structurally modified outside the iterator
They are two names for the same iterator behavior
Fail-fast iterators are guaranteed to detect every concurrent modification

questions.explanation: Fail-fast iterators, such as typical ArrayList iterators, make a best-effort check for structural modifications and may throw ConcurrentModificationException. Weakly consistent iterators, used by many concurrent collections such as ConcurrentHashMap, can operate while updates occur and may reflect some updates. Fail-fast behavior is not a correctness or synchronization guarantee.

questions.question: Why should mutable objects generally not be used as HashMap keys?

options.text: HashMap does not support object keys
Changing a key's fields that affect equals() or hashCode() can make the entry difficult to find in its original bucket
Mutable keys automatically cause ConcurrentModificationException
HashMap copies every key and makes it immutable

questions.explanation: HashMap uses a key's hash code to select a bucket and equality to locate the entry. If fields used by equals() or hashCode() change after insertion, subsequent lookups may search a different bucket or fail equality checks. Prefer immutable key types or ensure key state does not change while stored.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of common HashMap operations, and what can affect it?

options.text: get and put are always O(log n), regardless of implementation
get and put are average O(1), but collisions and resizing can affect performance; tree bins can improve heavily collided buckets
get is O(n) and put is always O(1)
All HashMap operations are O(n log n)

questions.explanation: HashMap get and put are expected O(1) under a well-distributed hash function. Collisions can increase lookup work; Java 8+ can treeify sufficiently large buckets, improving worst-case bucket lookup toward O(log n) when keys are appropriately comparable. Resizing is occasional O(n) work, while amortized insertion remains expected O(1).

questions.question: What is the difference between a `Thread` and a `Runnable` in Java?

options.text: Thread is an interface; Runnable is a class
Runnable is a functional interface defining the task; Thread is the execution unit — prefer Runnable/Callable over extending Thread to separate task from execution mechanism
They are identical — Thread implements Runnable
Runnable runs on the main thread; Thread runs on a new thread

questions.explanation: Prefer implementing `Runnable` (or `Callable<T>`) over extending `Thread` — it separates the task from how it runs, allows the class to extend something else, and works with ExecutorService. `Thread` is the actual OS-level thread abstraction. `Callable<T>` is like Runnable but returns a result and can throw checked exceptions.

questions.question: What does `synchronized` do in Java?

options.text: synchronized makes a method run on a separate thread
synchronized acquires the intrinsic lock (monitor) of an object before executing — ensuring only one thread executes that block at a time for the same object
synchronized makes all variables in a method thread-local
synchronized is equivalent to volatile

questions.explanation: Every Java object has an intrinsic lock (monitor). `synchronized(obj)` acquires that lock — other threads trying to synchronize on the same object block until it is released. `synchronized` method acquires `this` (instance methods) or `Class` (static methods). Provides mutual exclusion AND memory visibility (happens-before). Downside: reentrant but coarse-grained.

questions.question: What is `volatile` in Java and what guarantees does it provide?

options.text: volatile makes a variable thread-local — each thread gets its own copy
volatile guarantees visibility: reads and writes go directly to main memory (not CPU cache), and prevents instruction reordering around that variable — but does NOT guarantee atomicity
volatile is the same as synchronized — both provide mutual exclusion
volatile prevents a variable from being garbage collected

questions.explanation: `volatile` establishes a happens-before relationship: a write to a volatile variable happens-before all subsequent reads of that variable. This prevents stale cache reads. However, `volatile` does NOT make compound operations (like `i++`) atomic — `i++` is read-modify-write, three steps. Use `AtomicInteger` for atomic compound operations, `volatile` for simple flags and published references.

questions.question: What is `ExecutorService` and why should you use it over raw threads?

options.text: ExecutorService is deprecated — use virtual threads instead

ExecutorService is a thread pool abstraction that decouples task submission from execution, reuses threads, manages lifecycle, and handles rejection — more efficient and safer than creating raw Thread objects
ExecutorService is only useful for scheduled tasks
ExecutorService creates a new thread for every submitted task — same as new Thread()

questions.explanation: Raw threads are expensive to create. ExecutorService manages a pool of reusable threads. Key implementations: `newFixedThreadPool(n)` (fixed n threads), `newCachedThreadPool()` (expands/shrinks dynamically), `newSingleThreadExecutor()` (sequential). Always shut down: `exec.shutdown()` (wait for tasks) or `exec.shutdownNow()` (interrupt). `Future<T> f = exec.submit(callable)` for results.

questions.question: What is a `Future<T>` and what are its limitations?

options.text: Future represents a result that will be available later — get() blocks until complete; limitations: cannot compose, no callbacks, no exception handling without get()
Future is the same as CompletableFuture — no differences exist
Future is immutable — once set, the value cannot change
Future automatically retries failed computations

questions.explanation: `Future<T>` represents an async computation: `isDone()`, `cancel()`, `get()` (blocks), `get(timeout, unit)`. Limitations: blocking `get()`, no chaining/composition, no callbacks on completion, no easy exception handling. `CompletableFuture` (Java 8) solves all these limitations with a fluent, non-blocking API.

questions.question: What is `CompletableFuture` and how does it improve on `Future`?

options.text: CompletableFuture is just a Future that can be manually completed

CompletableFuture provides non-blocking async programming: thenApply (transform), thenAccept (consume), thenCompose (chain), allOf/anyOf (combine), exceptionally (error handling) — all without blocking
CompletableFuture is only for parallel streams
CompletableFuture replaces ExecutorService entirely

questions.explanation: `CompletableFuture` implements `Future` and `CompletionStage`. Key operations: `thenApply(fn)` transforms result, `thenAccept(consumer)` consumes it, `thenCompose(fn)` flat-maps, `thenCombine(other, fn)` combines two futures, `exceptionally(fn)` handles errors, `allOf(futures)` waits for all. Can specify executor for each stage.
questions.codeSnippet:
CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser(id))
  .thenApply(user -> enrichWithMetadata(user))
  .thenAccept(user -> cache.put(user.id(), user))
  .exceptionally(ex -> { log.error(ex); return null; });

questions.question: What is a `ReentrantLock` and when would you use it over `synchronized`?

options.text: ReentrantLock is slower than synchronized — only use synchronized

ReentrantLock provides explicit locking with additional features: tryLock() with timeout, lockInterruptibly(), fairness mode, multiple Condition objects — use when you need these features beyond what synchronized provides
ReentrantLock cannot be used with multiple threads — it is single-threaded
synchronized and ReentrantLock are identical in behavior

questions.explanation: `ReentrantLock` advantages: `tryLock()` — non-blocking attempt; `tryLock(timeout, unit)` — avoid deadlock with timeout; `lockInterruptibly()` — can be interrupted while waiting; fairness constructor `new ReentrantLock(true)` — FIFO ordering; multiple `Condition` objects (`lock.newCondition()`) for fine-grained `await`/`signal`. Must always unlock in `finally` to avoid lock leaks.

questions.question: What is a deadlock and how can you prevent it?

options.text: A deadlock is when a thread throws an exception while holding a lock
A deadlock occurs when two or more threads each hold a lock the other needs, waiting forever. Prevention: consistent lock ordering, tryLock with timeout, lock hierarchy, avoiding nested locks
Deadlocks only happen with ReentrantLock — synchronized cannot deadlock
A deadlock is automatically resolved by the JVM after 30 seconds

questions.explanation: Four conditions for deadlock (Coffman): mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Prevention: (1) Always acquire locks in the same order across threads. (2) Use `tryLock()` with timeout. (3) Avoid holding locks when calling external code. (4) Use higher-level abstractions (ConcurrentHashMap, Lock-free algorithms). Detect with `jstack` or thread dump analysis.

questions.question: What is `AtomicInteger` and how does it work without locks?

options.text: AtomicInteger is a thread-safe integer that uses synchronized internally
AtomicInteger uses Compare-And-Swap (CAS) CPU instructions for lock-free atomic operations — compareAndSet, getAndIncrement, etc. — eliminating lock overhead
AtomicInteger is only useful on multi-core machines
AtomicInteger wraps Integer with volatile — no CAS involved

questions.explanation: `AtomicInteger` uses the `sun.misc.Unsafe` class to call CPU-level CAS (Compare-And-Swap) instructions. CAS: 'if current value equals expected, swap to new value atomically; otherwise retry'. No locks, no blocking — threads spin briefly on contention. Operations: `getAndIncrement()`, `compareAndSet(expect, update)`, `getAndAdd(n)`. Java 8+: `LongAdder` is even better for high-contention counting.

questions.question: What is `ThreadLocal<T>` and when is it useful?

options.text: ThreadLocal creates a shared variable accessible by all threads
ThreadLocal provides per-thread storage — each thread has its own independent copy of the variable, avoiding synchronization
ThreadLocal is the same as volatile but restricted to local variables
ThreadLocal prevents a thread from accessing global state

questions.explanation: `ThreadLocal<T>` gives each thread its own copy via `get()` and `set(T)`. Common uses: database connections, SimpleDateFormat instances, security context (Spring's SecurityContextHolder), request-scoped data in web frameworks. Warning: thread pools reuse threads — always call `remove()` after use to prevent stale data leaking to the next request.

questions.question: What is `CountDownLatch` vs `CyclicBarrier`?

options.text: They are identical — both count down to zero and signal threads
CountDownLatch: one-time countdown, threads await until count reaches zero; CyclicBarrier: reusable — all threads meet at a barrier point before proceeding together
CyclicBarrier is for producers; CountDownLatch is for consumers
CountDownLatch is for single-threaded code; CyclicBarrier is for multithreaded

questions.explanation: `CountDownLatch(n)`: threads call `await()` to block until `countDown()` is called n times — one-shot, cannot be reset. Use case: wait for n services to start before serving requests. `CyclicBarrier(n, action)`: n threads each call `await()` — all block until all n have called it, then the optional action runs and the barrier resets. Use case: parallel computation with synchronization points.

questions.question: What is the Java Memory Model (JMM) and what is a happens-before relationship?

options.text: JMM defines how Java allocates heap memory for objects

JMM defines the rules for when one thread's writes are visible to other threads. Happens-before: if A happens-before B, A's effects are visible when B executes. Established by: synchronized, volatile, thread start/join, final fields
JMM is only relevant for garbage collection algorithms
JMM guarantees that all threads always see the latest values immediately

questions.explanation: Without synchronization, the JVM and CPU can reorder instructions for performance — another thread may see stale data. The JMM defines happens-before (HB): if action A HB action B, A's results are visible to B. Sources of HB: `synchronized` (unlock HB next lock), `volatile` (write HB subsequent reads), `Thread.start()` HB first action in thread, thread actions HB `Thread.join()` return.

questions.question: What is a `Semaphore` and what is it used for?

options.text: A Semaphore is a mutex that allows exactly one thread at a time
A Semaphore maintains a count of permits — acquire() takes a permit (blocks if 0); release() returns one. Used to limit concurrent access to a resource (e.g. connection pool, rate limiting)
A Semaphore is a thread-safe boolean flag
Semaphore is deprecated — use ReentrantLock instead

questions.explanation: `new Semaphore(n)` starts with n permits. `acquire()` decrements the permit count (blocking if 0). `release()` increments it. A Semaphore with 1 permit is a binary semaphore (mutex-like). Common uses: connection pool with max 10 connections (`new Semaphore(10)`), rate limiting, bounded access to shared resources. Unlike locks, permits don't need to be released by the same thread.

questions.question: What is `BlockingQueue` and what are its implementations?

options.text: BlockingQueue is a synchronized version of ArrayList

BlockingQueue is a thread-safe queue where put() blocks when full and take() blocks when empty — implementations: ArrayBlockingQueue (bounded), LinkedBlockingQueue (optionally bounded), SynchronousQueue (no storage), PriorityBlockingQueue
BlockingQueue only works between exactly two threads
BlockingQueue is deprecated — use ConcurrentLinkedQueue instead

questions.explanation: BlockingQueue is the backbone of the producer-consumer pattern. `put(e)` blocks if queue is full; `take()` blocks if empty; `offer(e, timeout, unit)` and `poll(timeout, unit)` are timeout variants. Implementations: `ArrayBlockingQueue(n)` (bounded, fair option), `LinkedBlockingQueue` (optionally bounded, more throughput), `SynchronousQueue` (no buffer — direct handoff), `PriorityBlockingQueue` (priority ordering).

questions.question: What are virtual threads (Project Loom, Java 21)?

options.text: Virtual threads are threads that run only in the JVM without OS involvement

Virtual threads are lightweight threads managed by the JVM (not OS threads) — millions can exist simultaneously because they unmount from OS threads while blocked, enabling high-concurrency without thread pool tuning
Virtual threads are the same as daemon threads
Virtual threads replace ExecutorService entirely in Java 21

questions.explanation: Traditional threads are OS threads (expensive: ~1MB stack, limited to ~thousands). Virtual threads (Java 21 GA) are JVM-managed — they mount on a carrier (OS) thread when runnable and unmount when blocked on I/O. Millions can exist simultaneously. Usage: `Thread.ofVirtual().start(runnable)` or `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()`. Ideal for I/O-bound workloads; don't use `synchronized` in virtual threads (use ReentrantLock to avoid pinning).

questions.question: What is `ForkJoinPool` and what is it designed for?

options.text: ForkJoinPool is a thread pool for I/O operations
ForkJoinPool is optimized for divide-and-conquer tasks using work-stealing — idle threads steal tasks from busy threads' queues, maximizing CPU utilization for CPU-bound recursive tasks
ForkJoinPool replaces BlockingQueue for producer-consumer patterns
ForkJoinPool is identical to FixedThreadPool but with a different API

questions.explanation: ForkJoinPool uses work-stealing: each thread has a deque of tasks; idle threads steal from the tail of busy threads' deques, minimizing contention. Used by parallel streams (`stream().parallel()`) and `CompletableFuture` (common pool). `RecursiveTask<T>` (returns result) and `RecursiveAction` (void) implement the fork-join pattern. The common pool is `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`.

questions.question: What is the difference between `wait()`/`notify()` and `Condition.await()`/`signal()`?

options.text: They are identical — just different APIs for the same mechanism
wait()/notify() use object monitors (tied to synchronized); Condition.await()/signal() work with ReentrantLock and support multiple conditions per lock, interruptibility, and timed waits
Condition.await() is deprecated — use wait() instead
notify() wakes all threads; signal() wakes only one

questions.explanation: `wait()`/`notify()`/`notifyAll()` must be called inside `synchronized` blocks and use the object's monitor. Limitations: one wait set per object, spurious wakeups require loops. `Condition` (from `lock.newCondition()`): multiple conditions per lock (e.g., `notFull` and `notEmpty` for a bounded queue), `awaitNanos()`, `awaitUntil()`, `awaitUninterruptibly()`. Always use in a `while` loop for both.

questions.question: What is `CopyOnWriteArrayList` and when should you use it?

options.text: CopyOnWriteArrayList is a synchronized ArrayList — same as Collections.synchronizedList()
CopyOnWriteArrayList creates a fresh copy of the backing array on every write — reads are always lock-free. Best for workloads with rare writes and frequent reads (listener lists, small caches)
CopyOnWriteArrayList should be used for high-write workloads for best performance
CopyOnWriteArrayList prevents ConcurrentModificationException by using a queue internally

questions.explanation: Every write to `CopyOnWriteArrayList` (add, set, remove) copies the entire backing array under a lock, then replaces the reference. Reads (iteration, get) use the old snapshot with no lock. Pros: zero-overhead reads, no ConcurrentModificationException during iteration. Cons: writes are O(n) and expensive. Best for: event listener lists, small collections with rare writes and many readers.

questions.question: What is `StampedLock` and how does it differ from `ReadWriteLock`?

options.text: StampedLock is a simplified ReadWriteLock with fewer methods

StampedLock supports optimistic reading — a read doesn't block writers, caller checks if a write occurred (validate stamp) and retries under a full read lock if so. Faster than ReadWriteLock for read-heavy workloads
StampedLock is deprecated — use ReentrantReadWriteLock instead
StampedLock only supports write locking

questions.explanation: `ReadWriteLock`: multiple concurrent readers OR one writer (readers block writers and vice versa). `StampedLock` adds optimistic reads: `tryOptimisticRead()` returns a stamp; after reading, `validate(stamp)` checks if a write occurred — if valid, no locking at all. If a write happened, fall back to a full read lock. Not reentrant. Best for read-dominated data structures.

questions.question: What is a race condition and how do you identify one?

options.text: A race condition is when threads compete for CPU time causing slowdowns
A race condition is when the program's behavior depends on the relative timing of thread executions — producing incorrect results that are hard to reproduce
A race condition always causes a deadlock
Race conditions only occur in languages without garbage collection

questions.explanation: A race condition occurs when: (1) two or more threads access shared mutable state concurrently, and (2) at least one access is a write, and (3) there is no synchronization. Classic example: `count++` is read-modify-write — two threads can both read 0, both write 1 instead of 2. Identification: hard to reproduce (timing-dependent), look for shared mutable state accessed without synchronization. Tools: thread sanitizers, code review.

questions.question: What is `ScheduledExecutorService` used for?

options.text: ScheduledExecutorService is for running one-time background tasks
ScheduledExecutorService schedules tasks to run after a delay or at fixed intervals — replacing Timer/TimerTask with a thread pool-backed, more reliable alternative
ScheduledExecutorService is a Calendar-aware scheduler for business hours
ScheduledExecutorService is deprecated — use cron expressions instead

questions.explanation: `Executors.newScheduledThreadPool(n)` returns a ScheduledExecutorService. Methods: `schedule(task, delay, unit)` — run once after delay; `scheduleAtFixedRate(task, initialDelay, period, unit)` — run repeatedly at fixed intervals (next run starts at period, regardless of previous duration); `scheduleWithFixedDelay` — fixed delay AFTER previous completion. Prefer over `Timer` which crashes all tasks if one throws.

questions.question: What does `Thread.sleep()` do and is it reliable for precise timing?

options.text: Thread.sleep() is precise to the nanosecond on modern JVMs
Thread.sleep(ms) causes the current thread to sleep at LEAST the specified time — the OS scheduler may wake it later. Not suitable for precise timing; use ScheduledExecutorService for periodic tasks
Thread.sleep() releases all locks held by the thread while sleeping
Thread.sleep() is the same as Object.wait() — both release the monitor

questions.explanation: `Thread.sleep(ms)` puts the thread in TIMED_WAITING state for at least `ms` milliseconds. The actual sleep time depends on OS timer granularity (typically 10-15ms on Windows). It does NOT release locks (unlike `wait()`). Throws `InterruptedException` if interrupted. For precise, reliable timing: use `ScheduledExecutorService.scheduleAtFixedRate()` or `LockSupport.parkNanos()`.

questions.question: What is the `Phaser` class in Java concurrency?

options.text: Phaser is a deprecated replacement for CountDownLatch
Phaser is a flexible synchronization barrier that supports dynamic participant registration, multiple phases, and optional termination — more flexible than CyclicBarrier
Phaser is a thread that runs in phases, sleeping between each
Phaser is used to coordinate phases of a build system

questions.explanation: `Phaser` extends CyclicBarrier and CountDownLatch capabilities: participants can `register()` and `deregister()` dynamically, `arriveAndAwaitAdvance()` waits at phase end, phase number advances on completion. Can be tiered (tree of Phasers) for massive parallelism. Override `onAdvance()` for phase-completion logic or to terminate. Rarely needed unless the flexibility is specifically required.

questions.question: What is the difference between `Thread.interrupt()` and `Thread.stop()`?

options.text: interrupt() stops a thread immediately; stop() requests cooperative termination
Thread.stop() is deprecated and unsafe (releases all locks, corrupts state); interrupt() is a cooperative signal — the thread checks isInterrupted() or handles InterruptedException to stop gracefully
They are identical — stop() just has a shorter name
interrupt() works on sleeping threads; stop() works on running threads

questions.explanation: `Thread.stop()` (deprecated Java 1.2) forcibly stops a thread, releasing all its locks and leaving shared state potentially inconsistent. `interrupt()` is cooperative: sets the interrupted flag on the target thread. The thread must check `Thread.interrupted()` or catch `InterruptedException` from blocking calls (sleep, wait, take). On catching InterruptedException, always restore the interrupt status or re-throw.

questions.question: What is `ThreadPoolExecutor` and what parameters does it take?

options.text: ThreadPoolExecutor is just another name for Executors.newFixedThreadPool()

ThreadPoolExecutor is the core implementation with parameters: corePoolSize, maximumPoolSize, keepAliveTime, workQueue, threadFactory, and rejectedExecutionHandler — used when factory methods don't meet requirements
ThreadPoolExecutor only supports a fixed number of threads
ThreadPoolExecutor is deprecated — use virtual threads instead

questions.explanation: Parameters: `corePoolSize` (threads kept alive even idle), `maximumPoolSize` (max threads), `keepAliveTime` (idle extra-thread timeout), `workQueue` (task buffer — `LinkedBlockingQueue`, `ArrayBlockingQueue`, `SynchronousQueue`), `threadFactory` (custom naming/daemon), `RejectedExecutionHandler` (AbortPolicy, CallerRunsPolicy, DiscardPolicy, DiscardOldestPolicy). Use over factory methods when you need bounded queues and custom rejection.

questions.question: What are the main states in the Java thread lifecycle?

options.text: NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, TERMINATED
CREATED, READY, EXECUTING, PAUSED, DESTROYED
NEW, RUNNING, SLEEPING, DEAD only
STARTED, LOCKED, FINISHED

questions.explanation: The Thread.State enum defines NEW, RUNNABLE, BLOCKED, WAITING, TIMED_WAITING, and TERMINATED. RUNNABLE includes a thread that may be executing or eligible to run; Java does not expose a separate RUNNING state. BLOCKED means waiting to acquire an intrinsic monitor lock.

questions.question: What is the difference between `wait()` and `sleep()`?

options.text: Both release every lock held by the current thread
`wait()` releases the monitor and must be called while owning it; `sleep()` pauses the current thread without releasing held monitors
`sleep()` releases the monitor; `wait()` does not
`wait()` is static and `sleep()` is an instance method

questions.explanation: Object.wait() must be called while the thread owns that object's monitor. It releases that monitor while waiting and reacquires it before returning. Thread.sleep() pauses the current thread for a time but does not release monitors it holds. wait() is commonly used with a condition predicate and notification; sleep() is not a synchronization mechanism.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `Thread.join()`?

options.text: It merges two thread objects into one
It makes the calling thread wait until the target thread terminates, optionally with a timeout
It interrupts the target thread immediately
It starts a thread if it has not been started

questions.explanation: Calling `join()` on a thread causes the current thread to wait until the target thread terminates. Overloads support waiting for a specified duration. It is commonly used when one thread must wait for another thread's work to finish. Calling join() does not start or interrupt the target thread.

questions.question: What are virtual threads in Java 21, and when are they useful?

options.text: They are OS threads with a larger default stack
They are lightweight threads managed by the JVM, useful for applications with many concurrent tasks that spend much of their time waiting
They automatically make CPU-bound algorithms faster through parallel execution
They replace synchronization and thread-safe data structures

questions.explanation: Virtual threads are lightweight threads scheduled by the Java runtime, allowing applications to support very large numbers of concurrent, mostly blocking tasks with a thread-per-task style. They are especially useful for I/O-bound workloads. They do not make CPU-bound work execute faster than available processors, and shared mutable state still requires proper coordination.

questions.question: What is the difference between `thenApply()` and `thenCompose()` in CompletableFuture?

options.text: `thenApply()` transforms a result; `thenCompose()` chains an asynchronous operation that itself returns a CompletionStage, flattening the nested stage
`thenApply()` handles exceptions; `thenCompose()` handles cancellation
`thenCompose()` always runs on a new thread; `thenApply()` always runs on the main thread
They are identical and interchangeable

questions.explanation: `thenApply()` applies a synchronous transformation to a completed result, producing a new stage. If the transformation returns a CompletableFuture, the result becomes nested. `thenCompose()` is analogous to flatMap: it applies a function returning a CompletionStage and flattens the result into one stage. Use it to sequence dependent asynchronous operations.

questions.question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions in Java?

options.text: Checked exceptions must be caught or declared; unchecked exceptions are RuntimeException subclasses and are not subject to that compile-time requirement.
Checked exceptions occur only at runtime; unchecked exceptions are detected by the compiler.
Checked exceptions are errors; unchecked exceptions are always recoverable.
There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable.

questions.explanation: Checked exceptions (for example, IOException) are checked by the compiler and must be caught or declared with throws. RuntimeException subclasses (for example, NullPointerException and IllegalArgumentException) are unchecked. Error represents serious JVM or environment problems and is also unchecked.

questions.question: What is the difference between `throw` and `throws`?

options.text: `throw` declares possible exceptions in a method signature; `throws` creates and raises an exception.
`throw` explicitly throws an exception object; `throws` declares exception types a method may propagate.
Both are used only inside catch blocks.
`throws` catches an exception, while `throw` suppresses it.

questions.explanation: Use `throw` followed by an exception instance to raise an exception, such as `throw new IllegalArgumentException("id")`. Use `throws` in a method or constructor declaration to state that exception types may propagate to the caller.

questions.question: When does a `finally` block not execute?

options.text: Whenever the try block completes normally.
Whenever a checked exception is thrown.
When the JVM or process terminates abruptly, such as through `System.exit()` or a fatal process failure.
Whenever a catch block handles an exception.

questions.explanation: A finally block normally runs whether the try block completes normally or abruptly, including when a catch block handles an exception. It is not guaranteed to run if the JVM exits or the process is forcibly terminated. Avoid relying on finally for actions that must survive process termination.

questions.question: What is try-with-resources, and what requirement must a resource meet?

options.text: The resource must extend Thread.
The resource must implement Serializable.
The resource must implement AutoCloseable (Closeable also qualifies).
The resource must be static.

questions.explanation: Try-with-resources automatically closes resources when control leaves the statement, including exceptional exits. A resource must implement `AutoCloseable`; `Closeable` extends `AutoCloseable`. This is preferred for files, streams, JDBC resources, and similar objects.

questions.question: If both the try body and `close()` throw exceptions in try-with-resources, what happens?

options.text: The exception from close always replaces the original exception.
The exception from the try body is primary; the close exception is attached as a suppressed exception.
Both exceptions are silently ignored.
The JVM combines them into a new RuntimeException.

questions.explanation: When the try body throws and closing also throws, the body exception remains the primary exception. The close failure is available through `Throwable.getSuppressed()`. This preserves the original failure while retaining cleanup diagnostics.

questions.question: What is the purpose of exception chaining?

options.text: To retry an operation automatically.
To preserve the original cause when translating an exception into a higher-level exception.
To prevent an exception from reaching the caller.
To convert every checked exception into an Error.

questions.explanation: Exception chaining preserves the underlying cause when an abstraction translates a low-level failure into a domain-specific exception. Use a constructor that accepts the cause, for example `new ServiceException("Unable to load account", cause)`. The stack trace then retains the causal context.

questions.question: Which statement about catch-block ordering is correct?

options.text: A superclass exception must be caught before its subclass.
Catch blocks can be placed in any order because Java selects the most specific automatically.
A subclass exception must be caught before a superclass exception, or the later catch is unreachable.
Only one catch block is allowed per try statement.

questions.explanation: Catch blocks are checked in order. A catch for a superclass such as `Exception` makes a later catch for `IOException` unreachable. Put more specific exception types before their supertypes. Multi-catch can handle unrelated exception types in one block.

questions.question: What restriction applies to the alternatives in a multi-catch clause?

options.text: The alternatives must be related by inheritance.
The alternatives cannot be related by subclassing; one cannot be a subtype of another.
Multi-catch supports only RuntimeException subclasses.
Multi-catch cannot catch checked exceptions.

questions.explanation: A multi-catch such as `catch (IOException | SQLException ex)` is valid because neither alternative is a subtype of the other. Related alternatives are rejected because the more specific type would be redundant. The multi-catch parameter is implicitly final.

questions.question: Why should application code generally avoid catching `Throwable`?

options.text: Throwable cannot be caught in Java.
It catches both Exception and Error, including serious conditions that applications usually should not attempt to handle.
It catches only checked exceptions.
It disables stack traces.

questions.explanation: `Throwable` is the root of the exception hierarchy and includes both `Exception` and `Error`. Catching it broadly can swallow serious JVM conditions such as `OutOfMemoryError`. Catch the narrowest types the application can meaningfully handle, and allow unrecoverable failures to propagate appropriately.

questions.question: What are the four pillars of Object-Oriented Programming?

options.text: Abstraction, Encapsulation, Inheritance, Polymorphism
Classes, Objects, Methods, Variables
Interfaces, Abstract classes, Enums, Records
Compilation, Interpretation, Execution, Garbage Collection

questions.explanation: The four OOP pillars: Encapsulation (bundling data + behavior, hiding internals), Inheritance (subclasses inherit from superclasses), Polymorphism (same interface, different behavior), Abstraction (hiding complexity, exposing only what's needed). These principles enable maintainable, reusable, and modular code.

questions.question: What is the difference between `==` and `.equals()` in Java?

options.text: They are identical — both compare object content
`==` compares object references (memory addresses); `.equals()` compares object content (unless overridden)
`.equals()` compares references; `==` compares content
`==` works for primitives only; `.equals()` works for objects only

questions.explanation: `==` checks if two references point to the same object in memory. `.equals()` checks logical equality — its default implementation (from Object) is also reference equality, but classes like String, Integer, and List override it to compare content. Always use `.equals()` for object comparison.

questions.question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in Java?

options.text: Abstract classes can have constructors and state; interfaces (pre-Java 8) could only have abstract methods — now interfaces can have default and static methods but cannot have instance state
Interfaces can be instantiated; abstract classes cannot
Abstract classes support multiple inheritance; interfaces do not
There is no difference — they are interchangeable

questions.explanation: Abstract class: can have constructors, instance fields, concrete methods, and abstract methods. A class can extend only one abstract class. Interface: no instance fields (only static final constants), all methods implicitly public. Since Java 8, interfaces can have `default` and `static` methods; since Java 9, `private` methods. A class can implement multiple interfaces.

questions.question: What does `final` mean when applied to a variable, method, and class?

options.text: Variable: immutable value; Method: cannot be overridden; Class: cannot be subclassed
Variable: null by default; Method: runs last; Class: abstract
All three mean the same thing — the element cannot be changed
Variable: thread-safe; Method: synchronized; Class: singleton

questions.explanation: `final` variable: its reference cannot be reassigned (but the object it points to can still be mutated unless the object itself is immutable). `final` method: cannot be overridden in subclasses. `final` class: cannot be extended (e.g., `String`, `Integer`). `static final` fields are compile-time constants by convention.

questions.question: What is method overloading vs method overriding?

options.text: Overloading: same method name, different parameters (compile-time); Overriding: subclass redefines superclass method (runtime)
Overloading: runtime polymorphism; Overriding: compile-time polymorphism
They are the same concept with different names
Overloading is for interfaces; Overriding is for abstract classes

questions.explanation: Overloading (static/compile-time polymorphism): same method name, different parameter types or count in the same class. The compiler decides which to call. Overriding (dynamic/runtime polymorphism): subclass provides its own implementation of a superclass method with the same signature. The JVM decides at runtime based on the actual object type.

questions.question: What is the difference between `String`, `StringBuilder`, and `StringBuffer`?

options.text: String: immutable, thread-safe; StringBuilder: mutable, not thread-safe (fast); StringBuffer: mutable, thread-safe (slower)
They are all immutable — only the syntax differs
StringBuilder is for single characters; StringBuffer is for multiple
String is deprecated; use StringBuilder or StringBuffer instead

questions.explanation: `String` is immutable — every concatenation creates a new object. `StringBuilder` is mutable and not synchronized — use in single-threaded code. `StringBuffer` is mutable and synchronized — use when shared across threads (but slow). In practice, use `StringBuilder` in loops and `String` for simple cases where the compiler already optimizes.

questions.question: What is the Java String pool and how does it affect memory?

options.text: The String pool is a network connection pool for database strings
The String pool is a special heap area where string literals are interned — JVM reuses existing String objects with the same value to save memory
The String pool stores all strings in native memory (off-heap)
The String pool is a fixed-size buffer that causes OutOfMemoryError when full

questions.explanation: String literals (e.g., `"hello"`) are automatically interned in the string pool. `String a = "hello"; String b = "hello"; a == b` is `true` because they reference the same pooled object. `new String("hello")` bypasses the pool, creating a new heap object. `String.intern()` manually adds a string to the pool. Since Java 7, the pool lives in the heap (was PermGen before).

questions.question: What is autoboxing and unboxing in Java?

options.text: Autoboxing is automatic type casting between numeric types
Autoboxing is the automatic conversion between primitive types (int, double) and their wrapper classes (Integer, Double); unboxing is the reverse
Autoboxing packages an object into a container class for shipping
Autoboxing and unboxing only apply to the String class

questions.explanation: The compiler automatically converts: `int i = 5; Integer boxed = i;` (autoboxing) and `Integer boxed = 10; int i = boxed;` (unboxing). Pitfalls: `Integer a = 1000; Integer b = 1000; a == b` is `false` (different objects). But `Integer a = 100; Integer b = 100; a == b` is `true` — Integer caches -128 to 127. Unboxing a null throws NullPointerException.

questions.question: What is the difference between `static` and instance members?

options.text: Static members belong to the class itself (shared across all instances); instance members belong to each individual object
Static members are thread-safe; instance members are not
Static methods can access instance variables; instance methods cannot access static variables
There is no difference — `static` is just an optimization hint

questions.explanation: Static members (fields, methods, nested classes) belong to the Class object — one copy shared across all instances, accessed via `ClassName.member`. Instance members belong to each object created with `new`. Static methods cannot access `this` or instance fields directly. Static initialization blocks run once when the class is loaded.

questions.question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions?

options.text: Checked exceptions must be declared or handled at compile time; unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException subclasses) do not
Checked exceptions crash the JVM; unchecked exceptions are recoverable
Unchecked exceptions must be caught; checked exceptions are optional
There is no difference — all exceptions behave the same

questions.explanation: Checked exceptions (IOException, SQLException) extend Exception but not RuntimeException. The compiler forces you to either catch them or declare `throws`. Unchecked exceptions (NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException) extend RuntimeException — no compiler enforcement. Rule of thumb: use checked exceptions for recoverable conditions a caller should handle; use unchecked for programming errors.

questions.question: What is the `this` keyword and what is `super` in Java?

options.text: `this` refers to the current object; `super` refers to the parent class
`this` refers to the class; `super` refers to the interface
Both refer to the current object — `super` just has higher priority
`this` is for methods; `super` is for constructors only

questions.explanation: `this` refers to the current instance — used to disambiguate fields from parameters (`this.name = name`), call another constructor in the same class (`this(...)`), or pass the current object. `super` refers to the parent class — used to call parent constructor (`super(...)`, must be first line), call overridden parent methods (`super.method()`), or access parent fields.

questions.question: What is the `instanceof` operator and what is pattern matching for instanceof (Java 16+)?

options.text: instanceof checks if an object is null
instanceof tests if an object is an instance of a type; pattern matching (Java 16+) combines the test and cast into one expression
instanceof is deprecated — use getClass() instead
instanceof only works with interfaces, not classes

questions.explanation: Traditional: `if (obj instanceof String) { String s = (String) obj; }`. Pattern matching (Java 16+): `if (obj instanceof String s) { }` — combines the check and cast, binding `s` in scope. Returns `false` for `null`. Used in `switch` expressions (Java 21 sealed classes + pattern matching).

questions.question: What are Java records (Java 16+) and what problem do they solve?

options.text: Records are a faster version of regular classes
Records are immutable data carrier classes that auto-generate constructor, getters, equals, hashCode, and toString from declared components
Records are Java's version of database records — they map to database rows
Records are deprecated classes that store legacy data

questions.explanation: `record Point(int x, int y) {}` auto-generates: canonical constructor, `x()` and `y()` accessor methods, `equals()`, `hashCode()`, and `toString()`. Records are implicitly `final` and cannot extend other classes. They make simple DTOs, value objects, and tuple-like structures much less verbose than equivalent POJOs.

questions.question: What are sealed classes in Java (Java 17+)?

options.text: Sealed classes are encrypted classes that require a license key
Sealed classes restrict which classes can extend or implement them — enabling exhaustive pattern matching
Sealed classes cannot be instantiated — they are like abstract classes
Sealed classes are final classes renamed for clarity

questions.explanation: `sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Rectangle, Triangle {}` — only the listed classes can implement Shape. Each permitted class must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`. Together with pattern matching switch, this enables exhaustive matching (compiler warns if a case is missing), similar to algebraic data types in functional languages.

questions.question: What is the difference between `int` and `Integer` in Java?

options.text: `int` is signed; `Integer` is unsigned
`int` is a primitive — stored directly on the stack; `Integer` is a wrapper object on the heap — can be null, used in collections
`Integer` is faster than `int` because it is pre-cached
They are identical — Java auto-converts them everywhere

questions.explanation: `int` (primitive): 4 bytes, stored on the stack (or in-object if a field), cannot be null, faster. `Integer` (wrapper class): an object on the heap, can be null, required for generics (`List<Integer>` not `List<int>`). Java's autoboxing converts between them automatically but with performance and NullPointerException risks.

questions.question: What is the difference between deep copy and shallow copy?

options.text: Shallow copy: copies primitive fields only; Deep copy: copies all fields including objects
Shallow copy: copies an object and its references (nested objects are shared); Deep copy: recursively copies all nested objects — fully independent
Deep copy uses clone(); Shallow copy uses the copy constructor
They are identical — Java always makes deep copies

questions.explanation: Shallow copy copies the object's fields. For reference fields, the copy and original share the same nested objects — mutating the nested object in one affects the other. Deep copy recursively copies all nested objects — fully independent. Java's `Object.clone()` is shallow by default. Implement deep copy via copy constructors, serialization, or a copying library (MapStruct).

questions.question: What are access modifiers in Java and what do they control?

options.text: public, protected, default, private — control memory allocation
public: accessible everywhere; protected: package + subclasses; default (no modifier): package only; private: class only
public, private, package, friend — control thread access
Access modifiers only apply to methods, not fields or classes

questions.explanation: From most to least restrictive: `private` (same class) → `default`/package-private (same package) → `protected` (same package + subclasses) → `public` (everywhere). Best practice: keep fields `private`, expose via getters/setters (encapsulation). Use the most restrictive modifier that works for your design.

questions.question: What is the contract between `hashCode()` and `equals()` in Java?

options.text: If two objects are equal via equals(), they must have the same hashCode()
hashCode() and equals() are independent — no contract exists
If two objects have the same hashCode(), they must be equal via equals()
hashCode() must always return a unique value for each object

questions.explanation: The contract: (1) If `a.equals(b)` is true, then `a.hashCode() == b.hashCode()` must be true. (2) The reverse is NOT required — objects with the same hashCode may not be equal (hash collision). If you override `equals()`, you MUST override `hashCode()`. Breaking this contract causes HashMap/HashSet to lose objects — they'd be stored but never found.

questions.question: What is a functional interface and what is `@FunctionalInterface`?

options.text: A functional interface is any interface in the java.util.function package
A functional interface has exactly one abstract method — the `@FunctionalInterface` annotation enforces this at compile time and enables lambda expressions
A functional interface is one that contains only static methods
A functional interface is deprecated — use abstract classes instead

questions.explanation: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). `@FunctionalInterface` causes a compile error if you accidentally add a second abstract method. Lambda expressions and method references are syntactic sugar for implementing functional interfaces. Built-in examples: `Runnable`, `Callable`, `Comparator`, and the `java.util.function` family.

questions.question: What is covariance and contravariance in Java generics?

options.text: Covariance: `List<Dog>` is a subtype of `List<Animal>` — this is how Java generics work by default
Java generics are invariant by default — `List<Dog>` is NOT a subtype of `List<Animal>`. Covariance uses `? extends T` (read-only); contravariance uses `? super T` (write-oriented)
Covariance and contravariance only apply to arrays, not generics
Covariance uses `? super T`; contravariance uses `? extends T`

questions.explanation: Java generics are invariant: `List<Dog>` is not a `List<Animal>` (unlike arrays which are covariant and type-unsafe). Wildcards add flexibility: `List<? extends Animal>` (covariant, read-only — producer) accepts `List<Dog>` or `List<Cat>`. `List<? super Dog>` (contravariant, write-oriented — consumer) accepts `List<Animal>` or `List<Object>`. Remember: PECS — Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

questions.question: What is type erasure in Java generics?

options.text: Type erasure deletes unused type variables from compiled bytecode
At runtime, generic type parameters are erased and replaced with Object (or the upper bound) — generic type information is only available at compile time
Type erasure is a security feature that prevents reflection from reading class types
Type erasure converts Java types to their C++ equivalents

questions.explanation: Java generics are a compile-time feature. The compiler checks types then erases them — `List<String>` becomes `List` in bytecode. Consequences: you cannot do `new T()`, `instanceof List<String>`, or create generic arrays `T[]`. At runtime, `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are the same class. This design maintained backward compatibility with pre-generics Java.

questions.question: What is the try-with-resources statement in Java?

options.text: A try block that automatically retries failed operations
A try block that automatically calls close() on declared resources when the block exits — even if an exception is thrown
A try block that allocates resources from a connection pool
A try block that catches all resource-related exceptions

questions.explanation: Any class implementing `AutoCloseable` (or `Closeable`) can be used in try-with-resources. `close()` is called automatically in the reverse order of declaration, even if an exception occurred — no finally block needed. If both the try body and `close()` throw, the close exception is suppressed (accessible via `getSuppressed()`).

questions.question: What are Java enums and how are they more powerful than constants?

options.text: Enums are just named integer constants — identical to public static final int
Enums are full classes: each constant is an instance, can have fields, constructors, and methods — plus type safety and built-in name/ordinal/values()/valueOf()
Enums cannot have methods — only constant values
Enums are deprecated in favor of sealed classes

questions.explanation: Java enums are full-featured classes. Each constant is a singleton instance. Enums can have fields, constructors, and methods. They support abstract methods (each constant provides its own implementation). Built-in: `values()` (all constants), `valueOf(String)`, `name()`, `ordinal()`. Safe for use in switch expressions. Can implement interfaces.

questions.question: What is the difference between `throw` and `throws` in Java?

options.text: `throw` declares exceptions; `throws` actually throws them
`throw` actually throws an exception instance; `throws` declares in the method signature which checked exceptions may propagate
They are identical — just different syntax for the same operation
`throws` is for runtime exceptions; `throw` is for checked exceptions

questions.explanation: `throw new IllegalArgumentException("msg")` — the statement that actually throws an exception at that point. `throws IOException` in a method signature — declares that the method may throw this checked exception, forcing callers to handle or propagate it. `throws` is part of the method contract; `throw` is the execution action.

questions.question: What are Java's primitive types and their sizes?
