options.text: byte(8), short(16), int(32), long(64), float(32), double(64), char(16), boolean(1)
byte(4), short(8), int(16), long(32), float(64), double(128), char(8), boolean(8)
All primitives are 32-bit — size depends on JVM implementation
Java has no primitive types — everything is an object

questions.explanation: 8 primitives: `byte` (8-bit, -128 to 127), `short` (16-bit), `int` (32-bit, most common integer), `long` (64-bit, suffix `L`), `float` (32-bit IEEE 754, suffix `f`), `double` (64-bit IEEE 754, default for decimals), `char` (16-bit Unicode, 0–65535), `boolean` (true/false, JVM-dependent size but logically 1 bit). Primitives are stored by value, not reference.

questions.question: What is the difference between a constructor and a method in Java?

options.text: A constructor initializes a new object and has the same name as its class; a method defines behavior and has a return type
A constructor must be static; a method must be final
Constructors are inherited by subclasses; methods are not
A constructor can be called only after an object has been created

questions.explanation: A constructor initializes an instance when it is created. It has the same name as the class and declares no return type, not even void. Methods represent behavior, have a declared return type (or void), and can be called after object creation. Constructors are not inherited, although a subclass constructor can invoke a superclass constructor using super().

questions.question: Why is String immutable in Java, and what are the practical benefits?

options.text: Immutability prevents strings from being garbage collected
Immutability supports safe sharing, string-pool reuse, stable hash codes, and safer use in security-sensitive APIs
Immutability means String objects are stored only on the stack
String is immutable only when declared with final

questions.explanation: A String's value cannot change after construction. Immutability makes strings safe to share across threads, enables reuse through the string pool, keeps hash codes stable for map keys, and reduces risks when strings represent paths, class names, or other security-sensitive values. Declaring a String reference final prevents reassignment of that reference; it is not what makes String immutable.

questions.question: What is the difference between `==` and `equals()` when comparing Java objects?

options.text: `==` compares object state; `equals()` compares memory addresses
`==` compares references for objects; `equals()` compares logical equality when the class overrides it
`equals()` always compares references, while `==` calls the object's hashCode()
They are interchangeable for all Java objects

questions.explanation: For reference types, `==` tests whether two references point to the same object. `equals()` is a method whose default implementation in Object also tests identity, but classes such as String override it to compare logical content. When overriding equals(), also follow the equals/hashCode contract.

questions.question: What is the purpose of `super()` in a Java constructor?

options.text: It creates a new instance of the current class
It invokes a constructor of the direct superclass
It invokes an overridden method in a subclass
It prevents the superclass from being initialized

questions.explanation: A constructor can invoke a superclass constructor with super(...). If no explicit constructor invocation is written, Java inserts a no-argument super() call when applicable. The superclass constructor runs before the subclass constructor body, ensuring inherited state is initialized first.

questions.question: What is the difference between `? extends T` and `? super T` in Java generics?

options.text: `extends` is generally used when reading values as T; `super` is generally used when adding T values
`extends` allows adding any object; `super` allows reading only Object
Both wildcards make a collection immutable
`super` is only valid for interfaces

questions.explanation: The PECS guideline means Producer Extends, Consumer Super. A `? extends T` reference is useful when a structure produces T values; you can safely read values as T, but generally cannot add a T because the actual subtype is unknown (apart from null). A `? super T` reference is useful when consuming T values; you can add T instances, while reads are typed as Object.

questions.question: Why are Java generics used?

options.text: To enable compile-time type safety and reduce explicit casts when working with parameterized types.
To make every collection automatically thread-safe.
To allow primitive types such as int as generic type arguments directly.
To execute code faster by eliminating all runtime type checks.

questions.explanation: Generics let classes, interfaces, and methods operate on types while preserving compile-time type checking. For example, `List<String>` prevents adding an Integer and returns String values without caller-side casts. Java generics use reference types; primitive type arguments require wrapper types such as Integer.

questions.question: What is type erasure in Java?

options.text: Generic type information is always stored in full at runtime for every object.
The compiler removes or replaces most generic type information during compilation, using bounds and casts as needed.
Java converts every generic type into a String.
Type erasure happens only when an application uses reflection.

questions.explanation: Java implements generics primarily through type erasure. The compiler enforces generic constraints, then erases type parameters to their bounds (or Object) and inserts casts where needed. This supports compatibility with pre-generics bytecode, but means `new T()` and `new List<String>[10]` are not allowed.

questions.question: What does `? extends Number` mean when used as a generic wildcard?

options.text: The type argument must be Number or a subtype of Number; values can safely be read as Number.
The type argument must be a supertype of Number.
The collection can accept any Object for insertion.
The wildcard means the collection is immutable.

questions.explanation: `List<? extends Number>` can refer to a List<Integer>, List<Double>, and so on. You can safely read elements as Number, but generally cannot add a Number because the actual element subtype is unknown (apart from null). This is an upper-bounded wildcard.

questions.question: What does `? super Integer` mean?

options.text: The type argument must be Integer or a subtype of Integer.
The type argument must be Integer or one of its supertypes, such as Number or Object.
The collection can only be read as Integer and cannot accept values.
The type argument must be an interface.

questions.explanation: `List<? super Integer>` may be a List<Integer>, List<Number>, or List<Object>. It can safely accept Integer values. When reading, the compiler can guarantee only Object. This is a lower-bounded wildcard and is useful for consumers of Integer values.

questions.question: What does the PECS guideline mean?

options.text: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.
Private Encapsulation, Public Serialization.
Parameterized Elements Cannot Share.
Producer Equals, Consumer Subclass.

questions.explanation: PECS means Producer Extends, Consumer Super. Use `? extends T` when a structure produces values for you to read as T; use `? super T` when it consumes T values you want to add. It is a practical guideline for choosing wildcard bounds.

questions.question: Why can you not create an array of a parameterized type such as `new List<String>[10]`?

options.text: Arrays are always immutable.
Arrays are covariant and reified at runtime, while generic type arguments are erased; combining them could undermine type safety.
List is not a valid array component type.
Java arrays cannot contain object references.

questions.explanation: Arrays know and enforce their component type at runtime and are covariant. Generic type arguments are erased, so the runtime cannot distinguish `List<String>` from `List<Integer>`. A generic array could therefore permit heap pollution. Java prohibits direct creation of generic arrays.

questions.question: What is a bounded type parameter, such as `<T extends Comparable<T>>`?

options.text: It restricts T to types that implement or extend the specified bound, enabling use of bound members.
It guarantees T is a primitive type.
It makes T immutable.
It declares that T must be exactly Comparable and cannot be a class.

questions.explanation: A bound constrains the permitted type arguments. `<T extends Comparable<T>>` allows code to call `compareTo` on T. A type parameter can have multiple bounds, with at most one class bound and that class bound appearing first.

questions.question: What is heap pollution in the context of Java generics?

options.text: When the heap runs out of memory.
When a variable of a parameterized type refers to an object that is not of that parameterized type, potentially causing a later ClassCastException.
When a generic collection contains duplicate elements.
When the garbage collector moves an object.

questions.explanation: Heap pollution occurs when a parameterized variable refers to an object that violates its compile-time generic type expectation. Unsafe raw types, unchecked casts, and some varargs operations can cause it. The failure may appear later at an implicit cast when an element is read.

questions.question: What is the difference between byte streams and character streams?

options.text: Byte streams process raw 8-bit bytes; character streams process text characters and handle character encoding through readers and writers.
Byte streams are only for network sockets; character streams are only for files.
Character streams are always faster than byte streams.
There is no difference in their intended use.

questions.explanation: InputStream and OutputStream APIs process bytes and are suitable for binary data. Reader and Writer APIs process character data and bridge bytes to characters using a charset. Choose based on whether the data is binary or text.

questions.question: Why is buffering used in Java I/O?

options.text: To encrypt data automatically.
To reduce the number of underlying read or write operations by transferring data in larger chunks.
To guarantee that every write reaches disk immediately.
To make a stream reusable after it is closed.

questions.explanation: BufferedInputStream, BufferedOutputStream, BufferedReader, and BufferedWriter keep data in memory buffers. This reduces expensive calls to the underlying source or destination. Buffering does not itself guarantee durable disk writes; flush or close as appropriate.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the `Path` and `Files` APIs in `java.nio.file`?

options.text: They replace Java collections with filesystem collections.
Path represents a filesystem path, while Files provides utility operations such as read, write, copy, move, and attribute access.
Path opens a database connection and Files executes SQL.
They are available only on Linux.

questions.explanation: `Path` models a path in a filesystem and is commonly obtained from `Path.of(...)`. The `Files` utility class performs operations such as `readString`, `writeString`, `copy`, `move`, `delete`, and directory traversal. These APIs are generally preferred over older File APIs for modern filesystem work.

questions.question: What is the difference between `File` and `Path`?

options.text: File is the newer API and Path is deprecated.
File is the older java.io abstraction; Path is part of NIO.2 and offers a richer path model and integration with Files.
Path can represent only existing files, while File can represent only directories.
File supports symbolic links but Path does not.

questions.explanation: `java.io.File` is an older abstraction with a limited API. `java.nio.file.Path` provides richer path manipulation and works with the `Files` class, filesystem providers, and operations such as resolving and normalizing paths. A Path can represent a path whether or not it currently exists.

questions.question: What is Java object serialization?

options.text: Converting an object graph into a byte stream for storage or transfer, traditionally using ObjectOutputStream and Serializable.
Converting Java source code into bytecode.
Converting every object into JSON automatically.
Encrypting objects with the JVM.

questions.explanation: Traditional Java serialization writes object state to a byte stream using ObjectOutputStream and reads it with ObjectInputStream. Serializable is a marker interface. Serialization has compatibility and security concerns; avoid deserializing untrusted data and consider explicit formats such as JSON or Protocol Buffers for many application protocols.

questions.question: What is the role of `serialVersionUID`?

options.text: It identifies the JVM process that serialized an object.
It is a version identifier used during deserialization to check serialization compatibility.
It encrypts serialized object data.
It determines the order in which fields are written.

questions.explanation: `serialVersionUID` is compared between the serialized stream and the local class during deserialization. If the identifiers are incompatible, InvalidClassException may be thrown. Explicitly declaring it makes versioning behavior more predictable than relying on a computed value.

questions.question: What is a `ByteBuffer` in Java NIO?

options.text: A thread-safe queue of bytes.
A container for bytes with position, limit, and capacity used in buffer-oriented I/O.
A wrapper around a database BLOB.
A character encoding table.

questions.explanation: ByteBuffer stores bytes and tracks `position`, `limit`, and `capacity`. Data is commonly written into a buffer, then `flip()` switches it for reading; after consumption, `clear()` prepares it for writing again. Channels transfer data to and from buffers.

questions.question: What is the difference between blocking and non-blocking I/O in NIO?

options.text: Blocking I/O always uses more CPU than non-blocking I/O.
In blocking I/O, an operation may wait for completion; non-blocking channel operations can return without waiting, allowing a thread to manage multiple channels.
Non-blocking I/O cannot be used with sockets.
Blocking I/O is asynchronous by definition.

questions.explanation: Blocking operations may wait until data is available or an operation completes. Non-blocking channels can return immediately when they cannot make progress; selectors can notify a thread when registered channels become ready. Non-blocking I/O is useful for scalable network servers but adds programming complexity.

questions.question: What is JDBC?

options.text: A Java API for connecting to relational databases and executing SQL statements.
A Java framework for building user interfaces.
A replacement for the Java Collections Framework.
A JVM garbage collector.

questions.explanation: JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) defines APIs for obtaining database connections, executing SQL, processing results, and handling transactions. A database-specific driver implements the JDBC interfaces.

questions.question: Why should `PreparedStatement` generally be preferred over `Statement` for parameterized SQL?

options.text: It automatically commits every transaction.
It supports bind parameters, helps prevent SQL injection when values are bound correctly, and can allow statement reuse.
It can execute only SELECT statements.
It eliminates the need for database indexes.

questions.explanation: PreparedStatement separates SQL structure from parameter values. Binding user input avoids treating those values as executable SQL syntax, mitigating SQL injection. It also provides typed setters and may benefit from database or driver statement preparation and reuse. Do not build SQL identifiers from untrusted input.

questions.question: What is the purpose of JDBC `ResultSet`?

options.text: To represent the rows returned by a query and provide cursor-based access to column values.
To configure the connection pool size.
To define database schema migrations.
To commit a transaction.

questions.explanation: A ResultSet represents tabular data returned by a query. Its cursor initially sits before the first row; calling `next()` advances it. Column values can be read by index or label using typed getter methods. Close it when finished, preferably with try-with-resources.

questions.question: What is JDBC auto-commit mode?

options.text: Every SQL statement is automatically committed as an individual transaction when auto-commit is enabled.
All SQL statements are rolled back when the connection closes.
It means the database does not use transactions.
It commits only SELECT statements.

questions.explanation: Connections commonly start with auto-commit enabled. In this mode, a statement is committed when it completes. To group multiple operations into one transaction, call `setAutoCommit(false)`, execute the work, then commit or roll back explicitly.

questions.question: What is the purpose of JDBC batch updates?

options.text: To execute a group of update statements together, potentially reducing round trips and improving throughput.
To make every statement execute in a separate database connection.
To guarantee that a batch is atomic on every database and driver.
To replace prepared statements.

questions.explanation: JDBC batching uses methods such as `addBatch()` and `executeBatch()` to submit multiple updates together. It can reduce network overhead. Transactional atomicity depends on transaction settings and database behavior; use an explicit transaction when all-or-nothing behavior is required.

questions.question: What does transaction isolation control?

options.text: Which database user can connect to the server.
How visible one transaction’s intermediate or committed changes are to concurrent transactions, and which concurrency anomalies are permitted.
How many columns a table can contain.
Whether SQL statements are prepared or compiled.

questions.explanation: Isolation levels define the visibility of concurrent transaction effects and trade consistency against concurrency. Common JDBC levels include READ_UNCOMMITTED, READ_COMMITTED, REPEATABLE_READ, and SERIALIZABLE. Exact anomaly guarantees and implementation details can vary by database.

questions.question: What is a connection pool and why is it used?

options.text: A cache of SQL query results that replaces the database.
A managed set of reusable database connections that avoids repeatedly creating physical connections and controls concurrent usage.
A collection of database tables stored in the JVM heap.
A mechanism that makes a single JDBC Connection safe for concurrent use by all threads.

questions.explanation: Creating physical database connections is relatively expensive. A connection pool such as HikariCP maintains reusable connections, limits concurrency, and provides connections to callers on demand. Applications should borrow a connection for a unit of work and return it promptly; they should not share one Connection concurrently across unrelated requests.

questions.question: What should an application do if one operation in a multi-step JDBC transaction fails?

options.text: Always commit the successful statements and ignore the failed one.
Roll back the transaction when the intended unit of work must be atomic, then handle or propagate the failure.
Close the JVM to force the database to roll back.
Switch auto-commit on before handling the error.

questions.explanation: For an all-or-nothing unit of work, disable auto-commit, execute the steps, and commit only when all succeed. On failure, roll back and propagate or translate the exception. Ensure resources are closed and understand that some database errors may mark the transaction as aborted until rollback.

questions.question: Why should JDBC resources be closed promptly?

options.text: Closing a ResultSet or Statement automatically deletes the underlying table.
Connections, statements, and result sets may hold database, network, and memory resources; closing them returns resources to the driver or pool.
Java refuses to garbage-collect objects that implement AutoCloseable.
Closing resources is required only for SELECT statements.

questions.explanation: JDBC resources can hold cursors, server-side handles, network resources, and pooled connections. Use nested try-with-resources or framework-managed transactions to close ResultSet and Statement and return Connection resources reliably, including on exceptions.

questions.question: What are the main components of the JVM architecture?

options.text: Compiler, Linker, Loader, Executor
Class Loader, Runtime Data Areas (heap, stack, method area, PC register, native method stack), Execution Engine (interpreter + JIT), and Native Interface
Front-end, Back-end, Middleware, Database
Parser, Lexer, Optimizer, Code Generator

questions.explanation: JVM components: (1) Class Loader: loads .class files into memory. (2) Runtime Data Areas: Method Area (class metadata, static fields), Heap (objects, GC managed), Stack (per-thread, frames for method calls), PC Register (per-thread, current instruction), Native Method Stack. (3) Execution Engine: Interpreter (line by line) + JIT compiler (hot code to native). (4) JNI: native method calls.

questions.question: What is the difference between the heap and the stack in Java?

options.text: Heap: thread-local, stores primitives; Stack: shared, stores objects
Stack: per-thread, stores method frames (local variables, operand stack, return address) — LIFO, fast; Heap: shared across threads, stores all objects — GC managed, slower
Heap is for static fields; Stack is for instance fields
They are the same memory region — just different names

questions.explanation: Stack (per-thread): each method call creates a frame with local variables, operand stack, and return address. Frame is popped when method returns. Fixed-size; StackOverflowError on deep recursion. Heap (shared): all objects live here (`new Object()`). GC reclaims unreachable objects. Escape analysis (JVM optimization) can allocate objects on the stack if they don't escape the method.

questions.question: What is JIT compilation and how does it improve Java performance?

options.text: JIT compiles Java source code to bytecode — same as javac
JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler monitors hot code paths at runtime and compiles bytecode to optimized native machine code — enabling Java to approach C++ performance for frequently executed code
JIT runs only once at application startup
JIT is disabled by default — enable with -XX:+UseJIT

questions.explanation: Java bytecode is interpreted by the JVM initially (slow). The JIT monitors execution frequency — 'hot' methods (called many times) are compiled to native machine code. Advanced optimizations: inlining (removes method call overhead), loop unrolling, escape analysis, dead code elimination, speculative optimization with deoptimization fallback. C1 compiler: fast compile, moderate optimization. C2: slower compile, aggressive optimization (production).

questions.question: What is Garbage Collection in Java and what is the generational hypothesis?

options.text: GC is a manual process — Java developers call System.gc() to collect garbage

GC automatically reclaims heap memory for objects with no reachable references. The generational hypothesis: most objects die young — GC exploits this by dividing heap into Young (Eden, S0, S1) and Old generations
GC runs every 30 seconds regardless of memory pressure
GC only runs when the JVM explicitly detects a memory leak

questions.explanation: Generational GC: Young Generation (Eden + Survivor spaces S0/S1) holds new objects. Minor GC collects Young Gen frequently and is fast. Objects surviving multiple minor GCs are promoted to Old Generation. Major/Full GC collects Old Gen — less frequent but more expensive. This exploits the fact that most short-lived objects (temp variables, closures) die before promotion.

questions.question: What is the difference between G1GC, ZGC, and the Serial/Parallel GC collectors?

options.text: They are identical — just different names for the same algorithm

Serial/Parallel GC: simple, throughput-focused, stop-the-world pauses. G1GC: low-pause, region-based (default Java 9+). ZGC/Shenandoah: ultra-low latency (<10ms pauses even for TB heaps), mostly concurrent collection
ZGC is only for garbage-collected languages other than Java
G1GC is the fastest for all workloads

questions.explanation: SerialGC: single thread, stop-the-world — for embedded/small heaps. ParallelGC: multiple threads, still stop-the-world — for throughput (batch jobs). G1GC (default): divides heap into regions, concurrent marking, predictable pause targets (default 200ms). ZGC (Java 15+): concurrent compaction, sub-millisecond pauses, colored pointers — for latency-sensitive apps. Choose based on your latency/throughput trade-off.

questions.question: What is the ClassLoader hierarchy in Java?

options.text: There is only one ClassLoader — the default system ClassLoader
Bootstrap ClassLoader (JVM core) → Platform/Extension ClassLoader → Application ClassLoader — parent delegation: a child always asks its parent first
ClassLoader is a single class that loads all classes alphabetically
Each package has its own ClassLoader

questions.explanation: Three-level hierarchy (Java 9+ module system): Bootstrap ClassLoader (native C++, loads `java.lang.*` etc.), Platform ClassLoader (loads JDK modules), Application ClassLoader (loads classpath). Parent delegation: when loading a class, the ClassLoader delegates to its parent first — only loads itself if the parent can't find it. Prevents malicious overriding of core classes. Custom ClassLoaders enable hot-reload, plugins, isolation.

questions.question: What is `OutOfMemoryError` and what are its common causes?

options.text: OutOfMemoryError means the disk is full

OutOfMemoryError is thrown when the JVM cannot allocate memory. Common causes: heap exhaustion (too many live objects), memory leaks, PermGen/Metaspace exhaustion (too many loaded classes), native memory exhaustion
OutOfMemoryError only occurs in multithreaded programs
OutOfMemoryError is recoverable — catch it and free some objects

questions.explanation: Common OOMError messages: `Java heap space` — too many live objects or a memory leak. `GC overhead limit exceeded` — GC spending >98% of time recovering <2% of heap. `Metaspace` (Java 8+) — too many loaded classes (common in OSGi/app servers). `Unable to create new native thread` — OS thread limit. `Direct buffer memory` — off-heap NIO buffers. Fix: heap analysis with JProfiler/MAT, increase -Xmx (short term), fix leak (long term).

questions.question: What is Metaspace and how does it differ from PermGen?

options.text: They are identical — Metaspace is just the Java 8+ name for PermGen

PermGen (Java 7-): fixed-size region in heap for class metadata — frequently caused OOMError. Metaspace (Java 8+): off-heap native memory, auto-grows (bounded by OS), much less likely to OOM for class metadata
Metaspace is larger than PermGen by default
Metaspace stores objects; PermGen stored class metadata

questions.explanation: PermGen was part of the heap with a fixed default size (64MB-256MB). Class metadata, interned strings, and static fields went there — hot spot for OOMError in app servers that reload classes. Java 8 removed PermGen and moved class metadata to Metaspace (native memory outside the JVM heap). Metaspace grows automatically up to OS limits. `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` sets a cap. Static fields and interned strings moved to the heap.

questions.question: What are GC roots and how does the GC determine which objects are alive?

options.text: The GC marks objects alive if their reference count is > 0

GC roots are objects the GC considers always reachable (thread stacks, static fields, JNI references). The GC traces references from roots — anything reachable is alive; unreachable objects are collected
The GC uses timestamps to determine which objects to collect
All objects created in the last 30 seconds are considered alive

questions.explanation: GC uses reachability analysis (tracing), not reference counting (which can't handle cycles). GC roots: local variables and method parameters on thread stacks, static fields, JNI global references, class objects of loaded classes, monitor references. The GC traces the object graph from roots — everything reachable is live. Everything unreachable (even if objects reference each other in a cycle) is collected.

questions.question: What are key JVM flags for tuning memory and GC?

options.text: -memory:size and -gc:algorithm are the only flags needed
-Xms (initial heap), -Xmx (max heap), -Xss (stack size), -XX:+UseG1GC, -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis, -Xlog:gc for GC logging
JVM memory cannot be configured — it adjusts automatically
Memory flags only work on Linux — Windows uses a different API

questions.explanation: Key flags: `-Xms512m` (initial heap 512MB), `-Xmx4g` (max heap 4GB), `-Xss512k` (thread stack size), `-XX:+UseG1GC` or `-XX:+UseZGC`, `-XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=200` (G1 pause target), `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=dump.hprof` (auto heap dump), `-Xlog:gc*:gc.log` (GC logging). Setting `-Xms`=`-Xmx` avoids heap resizing overhead in production.

questions.question: What is a soft reference, weak reference, and phantom reference?

options.text: They are identical — all prevent garbage collection
Soft: collected only under memory pressure (cache use case); Weak: collected at next GC regardless of memory (canonical maps); Phantom: collected after finalization, used for post-GC cleanup actions
All three allow GC to collect the referenced object immediately
They are different names for reference types in different Java versions

questions.explanation: Reference strength (from strongest to weakest): Strong > Soft > Weak > Phantom. `SoftReference<T>`: GC collects when memory is low — good for memory-sensitive caches. `WeakReference<T>`: GC collects at next GC cycle (used in WeakHashMap, listener registries). `PhantomReference<T>`: object is already finalized — use with ReferenceQueue to perform cleanup after GC (replacing finalizers). `WeakReference` is most commonly used in practice.

questions.question: What is `System.gc()` and should you call it?

options.text: System.gc() forces immediate garbage collection — call it to free memory
System.gc() is a hint suggesting the JVM run GC — the JVM may ignore it. Calling it in production is almost always wrong: it triggers expensive full GC, disrupts GC tuning, and rarely helps
System.gc() stops all threads and performs GC synchronously
System.gc() is removed in Java 17+

questions.explanation: Calling `System.gc()` in production code is an anti-pattern. The JVM is better at deciding when to GC. Explicit calls often cause unnecessary full GC (long stop-the-world pauses), degrade throughput, and interfere with GC tuning. The only legitimate use is in test code to verify finalizers/cleaners. If memory pressure is real, fix the memory leak or tune heap size.

questions.question: What is GraalVM and what is Ahead-of-Time (AOT) compilation?

options.text: GraalVM is a new Java programming language

GraalVM is a high-performance JVM with an advanced JIT compiler and native image support — AOT compilation compiles Java to a standalone native executable at build time, enabling near-instant startup and low memory footprint
GraalVM is Oracle's cloud platform for running Java applications
AOT compilation is the same as JIT — just done at a different time

questions.explanation: GraalVM Native Image compiles Java applications AOT to native binaries — no JVM needed at runtime. Benefits: millisecond startup (critical for serverless/Lambda), low memory (no JVM overhead). Limitations: slower peak throughput than JIT (no runtime profiling), static analysis requires closed-world assumption (challenges with reflection, dynamic class loading). Spring Boot 3+ and Quarkus support native compilation.

questions.question: What is a memory leak in Java and how do you detect it?

options.text: Memory leaks are impossible in Java — GC prevents them
A Java memory leak is when objects are still referenced (not eligible for GC) but no longer needed by the application — detected via heap dumps, memory profilers, and GC log analysis
A memory leak occurs only when native memory is used via JNI
Memory leaks in Java always cause OutOfMemoryError within seconds

questions.explanation: Java memory leaks: objects that are reachable but useless. Common causes: static collections holding objects (`static List<>`), listeners not unregistered (event bus, GUI), ThreadLocal not cleaned in thread pools, cache without eviction policy, unclosed streams/connections (pre-try-with-resources). Detection: heap dump with `jmap -dump` or `-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError`, then analyze with Eclipse MAT or JProfiler.

questions.question: What are `finalize()` and `Cleaner` — when was finalize() deprecated?

options.text: finalize() is the recommended way to release resources — use it in all classes
finalize() is called by GC before collecting an object — deprecated in Java 9, removed in Java 18. Use try-with-resources and Cleaner (Java 9+) for resource cleanup instead
Cleaner is deprecated; finalize() is the modern replacement
finalize() runs immediately when an object goes out of scope

questions.explanation: `finalize()` problems: unpredictable execution time (GC decides), can resurrect objects, prevents GC (finalizable objects need two GC cycles), degrades throughput. Deprecated Java 9, marked for removal. Java 9+ `Cleaner` API: register a cleaning action run after GC. Best practice: use `AutoCloseable` + try-with-resources for deterministic cleanup; use `Cleaner` as a safety net only.

questions.question: What happens during the class loading process in Java?

options.text: Class loading just copies .class bytes into memory
Class loading has three phases: Loading (find and read .class bytes), Linking (Verification + Preparation + Resolution), Initialization (run static initializers and assign static field values)
Class loading compiles .java files to bytecode
Class loading only happens once at JVM startup

questions.explanation: Class lifecycle: (1) Loading: ClassLoader reads .class bytes. (2) Linking: Verification (bytecode safe?), Preparation (allocate static fields, set defaults), Resolution (resolve symbolic references to actual classes). (3) Initialization: run static initializers and static field assignments in textual order. A class is initialized when first used (first instance created, static method called, static field accessed).

questions.question: What is the difference between `-Xms` and `-Xmx` and why would you set them equal?

options.text: -Xms is for minimum threads; -Xmx is for maximum threads
-Xms sets initial heap size; -Xmx sets maximum. Setting them equal avoids heap resizing (which pauses the JVM to expand/shrink) — common in production for predictable performance
Setting -Xms=-Xmx prevents the GC from running
They can only be set equal for embedded systems

questions.explanation: When heap needs to grow beyond `-Xms`, the JVM requests more OS memory (may cause pauses). When below some threshold, the JVM releases memory back. In production: set `-Xms` = `-Xmx` to prevent this resizing overhead — the heap is pre-allocated at startup, eliminating mid-run pauses from heap expansion. Trade-off: consumes the full heap memory even if the app doesn't need it all.

questions.question: What is bytecode and how does the JVM execute it?

options.text: Bytecode is binary machine code specific to one CPU architecture
Bytecode is an intermediate representation compiled from Java source — platform-independent, executed by the JVM interpreter or compiled to native code by JIT
Bytecode is the compressed version of Java source code
The JVM compiles bytecode back to Java source before executing

questions.explanation: Java compiles to bytecode (.class files) — a stack-based instruction set for the JVM (not for any real CPU). `javap -c MyClass` disassembles bytecode. The JVM interprets bytecode first, then JIT compiles hot methods to native machine code for the target CPU. This is the foundation of Java's 'write once, run anywhere' promise — the same bytecode runs on any JVM.

questions.question: What is escape analysis in the JVM?

options.text: Escape analysis is a technique to detect infinite loops
Escape analysis determines whether an object's reference escapes a method or thread — if not, the JVM can allocate it on the stack (no GC overhead), eliminate synchronization, or scalar-replace it
Escape analysis prevents memory leaks by detecting leaked references
Escape analysis is a static analysis tool run at compile time

questions.explanation: If an object doesn't escape the method that created it, the JIT can: (1) Stack allocate it (no heap allocation, no GC). (2) Eliminate synchronization on the object (lock elision — `synchronized` on non-escaped object is a no-op). (3) Scalar replacement: replace object fields with individual local variables. This is why `new StringBuilder()` in a method doesn't always create a heap object. Enabled by default in HotSpot.

questions.question: What is `jstack`, `jmap`, and `jstat` used for?

options.text: jstack is a build tool; jmap is a deployment tool; jstat is a testing tool
jstack: takes a thread dump (deadlock analysis, thread states); jmap: heap dump/histogram; jstat: GC statistics (heap usage, GC count/time) — all are JDK diagnostic tools for running JVM processes
They are obsolete tools replaced by Java Flight Recorder
jstack, jmap, and jstat only work on Linux servers

questions.explanation: `jstack <pid>`: prints thread dump — all thread states, stack traces, locked objects. Essential for diagnosing deadlocks, hung threads. `jmap -heap <pid>`: heap summary. `jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid>`: heap dump for MAT analysis. `jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000`: GC statistics every second. Modern alternative: Java Flight Recorder + JDK Mission Control (lower overhead, richer data).

questions.question: What is the difference between `StackOverflowError` and `OutOfMemoryError`?

options.text: Both indicate the same condition — JVM ran out of memory
StackOverflowError: thread's call stack exceeded its limit (deep recursion, infinite recursion); OutOfMemoryError: heap exhausted (too many live objects) or other memory region full
StackOverflowError is recoverable; OutOfMemoryError is always fatal
OutOfMemoryError is for heap; StackOverflowError is for Metaspace

questions.explanation: `StackOverflowError`: each thread has a stack (default 512KB-1MB). Deep or infinite recursion consumes stack frames until the limit is hit. Fix: add base case to recursion, convert to iteration, or increase `-Xss`. `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`: heap full — too many live objects or memory leak. Both are `Error` subclasses (not `Exception`) and should not normally be caught.

questions.question: What is the Module System (JPMS) introduced in Java 9?

options.text: JPMS is the Java Package Management System — similar to npm
JPMS (Project Jigsaw) introduces modules — named sets of packages with explicit requires/exports declarations, enabling strong encapsulation, reliable configuration, and a modular JDK
JPMS is a dependency injection framework built into Java 9
JPMS replaces ClassLoaders with a module-based loading system

questions.explanation: module-info.java: `module com.myapp { requires java.sql; exports com.myapp.api; }`. Benefits: (1) Strong encapsulation — internal packages are truly hidden (no reflection access without `opens`). (2) Reliable configuration — missing modules detected at startup, not runtime. (3) Smaller JDK: `jlink` creates custom runtime images with only needed modules. The JDK itself is now modular (java.base, java.sql, etc.).

questions.question: What is `invokedynamic` bytecode instruction and how does it relate to lambdas?

options.text: invokedynamic is the bytecode for dynamic class loading
invokedynamic allows the JVM to defer method dispatch to user-defined logic (bootstrap method) at runtime — Java uses it for lambda expressions, method references, and string concatenation
invokedynamic is only used by the Groovy and Kotlin languages
invokedynamic is identical to invokeinterface

questions.explanation: Added in Java 7, leveraged by Java 8 lambdas. When a lambda is first executed, `invokedynamic` calls a bootstrap method (in `LambdaMetafactory`) which generates a class at runtime implementing the functional interface. This is faster than generating anonymous inner classes at compile time (which was the pre-Java 8 approach). Also used by Kotlin, Groovy, JRuby for dynamic dispatch.

questions.question: What is the String constant pool and where does it live in Java 8+?

options.text: The String pool lives in PermGen in all Java versions
The String pool (interned strings) was moved from PermGen to the main heap in Java 7, remaining in the heap for Java 8+. This allows the GC to collect interned strings that are no longer referenced
The String pool lives in Metaspace in Java 8+
The String pool is stored in native memory outside the JVM

questions.explanation: Java 6 and earlier: String pool in PermGen (fixed size, OOM if too many unique literals). Java 7+: String pool moved to the heap (GC can collect unreferenced strings). Java 8: PermGen replaced by Metaspace, but the String pool stays on the heap. `String.intern()` adds a string to the pool. The pool enables `"hello" == "hello"` to be true (same pooled object reference).

questions.question: What is the difference between `Xss` (stack size) and thread stack overflow?

options.text: Xss controls the heap size; stack overflow is unrelated

`-Xss` sets each thread's stack size (default ~512KB-1MB). Stack overflow occurs when a thread's call stack exceeds this limit — usually from deep recursion. Increase `-Xss` for deep recursion, but investigate infinite recursion first
`-Xss` is the maximum string size; not related to thread stacks
Stack overflow can be prevented by setting `-Xss=0`

questions.explanation: Each thread in Java has its own stack allocated when the thread is created. Default size: ~512KB (Linux 64-bit JVM, varies by platform). `StackOverflowError` when a thread exhausts its stack. Increase with `-Xss2m` (2MB per thread). Warning: with many threads, this multiplies — 1000 threads × 2MB = 2GB of memory just for stacks. Investigate deep recursion and convert to iteration first.

questions.question: What is the difference between JDK, JRE, and JVM?

options.text: JVM executes bytecode; JRE provides the JVM and runtime libraries; JDK includes development tools plus the runtime
JDK executes only JavaScript; JRE compiles Java; JVM packages applications
JVM includes the compiler and debugger; JDK is only the runtime
They are three names for the same product

questions.explanation: The JVM is the virtual machine that loads and executes Java bytecode. A Java Runtime Environment traditionally consists of the JVM and libraries needed to run Java applications. The JDK includes the runtime components plus development tools such as the compiler. Since Java 9, Oracle/OpenJDK distributions are modular and do not always ship a separately named JRE.

questions.question: When does an object become eligible for garbage collection?

options.text: As soon as its constructor finishes
When it is no longer reachable from any GC root through strong references
When its reference count reaches zero
Whenever System.gc() is called

questions.explanation: An object is eligible for collection when it is no longer reachable through strong-reference paths from garbage-collection roots, such as active thread stacks, static references, and JNI references. Eligibility does not mean collection happens immediately. Java garbage collectors generally use reachability analysis rather than simple reference counting.

questions.question: What is a stop-the-world pause in the JVM?

options.text: A pause in which the JVM permanently stops all application threads
A period when application threads are paused so the JVM can perform certain operations safely, including some GC phases
A pause that occurs only when the heap is full
A mechanism that stops the operating system

questions.explanation: A stop-the-world (STW) pause suspends application threads at a safepoint so the JVM can perform operations requiring a stable view of application state. Garbage collection may include STW phases, although modern collectors such as G1 and ZGC aim to reduce pause duration and perform substantial work concurrently.

questions.question: What is a Java safepoint?

options.text: A location in source code where developers must call System.gc()
A JVM execution state at which threads can be safely paused for certain runtime operations
A special heap region reserved for static variables
A point at which an object is guaranteed to be garbage collected

questions.explanation: A safepoint is a coordinated state where application threads have reached locations at which the JVM can safely suspend them and inspect or modify runtime state. Operations such as some garbage collection phases, deoptimization, and thread stack inspection may require safepoints. Safepoint reachability and pause behavior are important JVM performance topics.

questions.question: What is the difference between minor, major, and full garbage collection terminology?

options.text: These terms have one fixed meaning across every JVM collector
They describe different collection scopes, but exact meanings and behavior depend on the garbage collector and JVM implementation
Minor GC always collects the entire heap
Full GC only collects objects in the stack

questions.explanation: Historically, minor GC commonly refers to collecting the young generation, while major GC often refers to old-generation collection and full GC to broader heap collection. However, terminology and exact behavior vary by collector and JVM version. When diagnosing performance, identify the collector in use and inspect its documented GC logs rather than relying only on these labels.

questions.question: What is the Spring IoC container and what problem does it solve?

options.text: IoC container is Spring's built-in web server

IoC (Inversion of Control) container manages object lifecycle and wires dependencies automatically — instead of objects creating their dependencies, the container injects them, enabling loose coupling and testability
IoC container is a database connection pool manager
IoC stands for Input/Output Connector — it manages file I/O

questions.explanation: Without IoC: `new UserService(new UserRepository(new DataSource(...)))` — classes are tightly coupled. With IoC: the container reads configuration (annotations, XML, Java config) and creates and wires beans. You receive dependencies injected, not created. Benefits: loose coupling (swap implementations), easier testing (inject mocks), centralized lifecycle management.

questions.question: What are the three types of dependency injection in Spring?

options.text: Field injection, setter injection, constructor injection — Spring supports all three
XML injection, annotation injection, Java config injection
Bean injection, service injection, repository injection
Singleton injection, prototype injection, request injection

questions.explanation: (1) Constructor injection: `@Autowired` on constructor (recommended) — dependencies are required, enables final fields, easy to test. (2) Setter injection: `@Autowired` on setter — optional dependencies, allows late injection. (3) Field injection: `@Autowired` on field (least recommended) — hides dependencies, harder to test without Spring. Spring team recommends constructor injection for mandatory dependencies.

questions.question: What are Spring bean scopes?

options.text: Spring beans have only one scope: singleton
Singleton (default, one instance per container), Prototype (new instance each time), Request (per HTTP request), Session (per HTTP session), Application (per ServletContext)
Spring beans use Java's scope rules (local, instance, static)
Bean scope determines which package the bean is visible in

questions.explanation: `@Scope("singleton")` (default): one shared instance per ApplicationContext. `@Scope("prototype")`: new instance on each `getBean()` call — Spring doesn't manage its full lifecycle after creation. `@Scope("request")`, `@Scope("session")`, `@Scope("application")`: web-only scopes. Caution: injecting a prototype bean into a singleton won't give a new prototype each time — use `Provider<T>` or `@Lookup`.

questions.question: What is Spring AOP and what is an Aspect?

options.text: AOP (Aspect-Oriented Programming) allows separating cross-cutting concerns (logging, transactions, security) from business logic via Aspects — applied transparently using proxies
AOP is Spring's API for Object Persistence
AOP is a testing framework for Spring beans
Aspects are Spring's name for configuration classes

questions.explanation: AOP terminology: Aspect (module of cross-cutting concern), Advice (action at a join point: Before, After, Around, AfterReturning, AfterThrowing), JoinPoint (method execution), Pointcut (expression selecting join points), Weaving (applying aspects). Spring AOP uses JDK dynamic proxies (interface-based) or CGLIB (class-based). `@Transactional` is AOP under the hood.

questions.question: What does `@Transactional` do in Spring?

options.text: @Transactional marks a class as a database entity
@Transactional wraps the method in a database transaction — starting one if none exists, committing on success, rolling back on RuntimeException (by default)
@Transactional is required for all Spring service methods
@Transactional makes a method thread-safe

questions.explanation: Spring wraps `@Transactional` methods in a proxy. Default propagation: `REQUIRED` (join existing transaction or create new). Rollback triggers: `RuntimeException` (unchecked) by default — not checked exceptions unless `rollbackFor = Exception.class`. Common gotchas: (1) self-invocation bypasses proxy — @Transactional won't fire. (2) Method must be `public` (proxy limitation). (3) Exception must propagate — don't swallow it.

questions.question: What is Spring Boot auto-configuration and how does it work?

options.text: Auto-configuration compiles Spring applications automatically without `javac`

Auto-configuration detects classes/jars on the classpath and automatically creates beans with sensible defaults — if you add spring-boot-starter-data-jpa, a DataSource, EntityManagerFactory, and TransactionManager are configured automatically
Auto-configuration generates Spring XML configuration from code
Auto-configuration is disabled by default — enable with @EnableAutoConfiguration

questions.explanation: `@SpringBootApplication` includes `@EnableAutoConfiguration`. Spring Boot scans `spring.factories` (or `AutoConfiguration.imports` in Boot 3+) for `@Configuration` classes with `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` etc. If DataSource class is on classpath and no DataSource bean exists, it creates one from `application.properties`. You can override any auto-configured bean by defining your own.

questions.question: What is the difference between `@Controller` and `@RestController`?

options.text: @Controller is for traditional MVC (returns view names); @RestController is @Controller + @ResponseBody — methods return data serialized to JSON/XML directly
@RestController is for microservices; @Controller is for monoliths
@Controller requires XML configuration; @RestController uses annotations
They are identical — @RestController is just a shorter alias

questions.explanation: `@Controller` marks a class as a Spring MVC controller. Methods return view names (resolved by ViewResolver) by default. Add `@ResponseBody` to a method to return data as response body. `@RestController` = `@Controller` + `@ResponseBody` on the class — all methods return data directly (JSON via Jackson by default). Use `@Controller` for server-side rendering (Thymeleaf), `@RestController` for REST APIs.

questions.question: What are `@RequestMapping`, `@GetMapping`, `@PostMapping` and related annotations?

options.text: @RequestMapping is for GET; @GetMapping is for POST — they handle different HTTP methods
@RequestMapping maps HTTP requests to methods (can specify method). @GetMapping, @PostMapping, @PutMapping, @DeleteMapping, @PatchMapping are shortcuts for specific HTTP methods
They are only for WebSocket endpoints
@RequestMapping is deprecated — only use @GetMapping and @PostMapping

questions.explanation: `@RequestMapping(value="/users", method=RequestMethod.GET)` is the general form. `@GetMapping("/users")` is the shortcut. Can be combined with `@RequestParam`, `@PathVariable`, `@RequestBody`, `@RequestHeader`. At class level, `@RequestMapping("/api/v1")` sets a base path for all methods in the controller.

questions.question: What is Spring Data JPA and what does `JpaRepository` provide?

options.text: Spring Data JPA is a standalone ORM framework separate from Hibernate
Spring Data JPA generates repository implementations at runtime from interface declarations — JpaRepository provides CRUD operations, pagination, sorting, and derived query methods
JpaRepository requires writing SQL queries for all operations
Spring Data JPA only works with PostgreSQL

questions.explanation: `JpaRepository<T, ID>` provides: `save()`, `findById()`, `findAll()`, `delete()`, `count()`, pagination (`findAll(Pageable)`), sorting. Derived queries: `findByEmailAndStatus(String email, Status status)` — Spring generates the JPQL automatically from the method name. `@Query("SELECT u FROM User u WHERE ...")` for custom JPQL. `@Modifying` for update/delete queries.

questions.question: What is `application.properties` vs `application.yml` and how does Spring Boot load configuration?

options.text: application.properties is for production; application.yml is for development

Both configure Spring Boot properties — .yml has hierarchical structure. Spring Boot loads: default → profile-specific (application-{profile}.yml) → external. @Value and @ConfigurationProperties bind values to beans
Only application.properties is supported — .yml requires a separate library
application.yml overrides application.properties only when both exist

questions.explanation: Spring Boot loads configuration in priority order (later overrides earlier): default properties → application.properties/yml → profile-specific → command line args → environment variables. `@Value("${server.port:8080}")` injects a property with default. `@ConfigurationProperties(prefix="app")` binds a whole config subtree to a POJO. Profiles: `spring.profiles.active=prod` loads `application-prod.yml`.

questions.question: What is Spring Boot Actuator?

options.text: Actuator is Spring's database connection pool
Spring Boot Actuator provides production-ready monitoring endpoints: /actuator/health, /actuator/metrics, /actuator/env, /actuator/beans, /actuator/loggers — all over HTTP or JMX
Actuator is Spring's AOP implementation
Actuator is a security module for authentication

questions.explanation: Add `spring-boot-starter-actuator`. Default endpoint: `/actuator/health` (integration with load balancer health checks). Key endpoints: `/actuator/metrics/jvm.memory.used` (Micrometer metrics), `/actuator/env` (all properties), `/actuator/beans` (all Spring beans), `/actuator/loggers` (change log levels at runtime), `/actuator/threaddump`, `/actuator/heapdump`. Secure in production: expose only health by default, use Spring Security to protect others.

questions.question: What is `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, and `@Controller` — are they different?

options.text: They are completely different annotations with distinct behaviors

@Component is the generic stereotype. @Service, @Repository, @Controller are specializations — all trigger component scanning and bean creation. @Repository additionally enables JPA exception translation
@Service creates beans with prototype scope; @Component creates singletons
@Repository is for MongoDB; @Component is for SQL databases

questions.explanation: All are `@Component` specializations — detected by component scanning (`@ComponentScan`). Semantic differences: `@Service` (business logic — no extra behavior). `@Repository` (data access — enables Spring's PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor to translate native exceptions to Spring's DataAccessException hierarchy). `@Controller` (Spring MVC — enables request mapping processing). Use the most specific one for documentation and tooling.

questions.question: What is `@Bean` vs `@Component` in Spring?

options.text: @Bean is deprecated; use @Component instead

@Component is a class-level annotation for Spring to manage; @Bean is a method-level annotation in a @Configuration class — used when you don't own the class (third-party) or need fine-grained creation control
@Bean creates prototype beans; @Component creates singletons
@Bean requires the class to implement BeanFactory

questions.explanation: `@Component` (and stereotypes) annotate classes you own — Spring instantiates them via component scanning. `@Bean` annotates methods in `@Configuration` classes — Spring calls the method and registers the return value as a bean. Use `@Bean` for: third-party classes you can't annotate, complex creation logic, conditional bean registration. Both are singleton by default.

questions.question: What is Spring Security and how do you configure basic authentication?

options.text: Spring Security is only for OAuth2 and JWT — not for basic auth

Spring Security is a framework for authentication and authorization — auto-configures HTTP Basic and form login. Customize by extending WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter (pre-Boot 2.7) or using SecurityFilterChain bean (Boot 3+)
Spring Security requires a database to store user credentials
Spring Security is disabled by default — must be explicitly enabled

questions.explanation: Spring Boot auto-configures Spring Security if on classpath (generates a random password, enables HTTP Basic). Customize with a `SecurityFilterChain` bean: configure which endpoints require auth, which permit all, CSRF settings, session management, and authentication (in-memory, JDBC, LDAP, OAuth2). Use `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` for method-level security.

questions.question: What is `@Conditional` and how does Spring Boot use it for auto-configuration?

options.text: @Conditional is used to create conditional branches in business logic

@Conditional creates beans only when specified conditions are met. Spring Boot uses: @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty, @ConditionalOnWebApplication — enabling smart auto-configuration
@Conditional is deprecated — use @Profile instead
@Conditional only works with @Component, not @Bean

questions.explanation: Spring Boot's auto-configuration is built entirely on `@Conditional` variants: `@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)` — configure JPA only if DataSource is on classpath. `@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)` — don't override if user defined their own. `@ConditionalOnProperty("feature.enabled")` — activate by property. `@ConditionalOnWebApplication` — only in web context. Create your own conditions by implementing `Condition`.

questions.question: What is `ResponseEntity<T>` in Spring MVC?

options.text: ResponseEntity is Spring's database response wrapper
ResponseEntity<T> represents a full HTTP response: status code, headers, and body — used when you need control over the response beyond just the body
ResponseEntity is required for all REST endpoints
ResponseEntity is deprecated — use @ResponseStatus instead

questions.explanation: `ResponseEntity<User>` lets you set HTTP status, headers, and body: `ResponseEntity.ok(user)` (200 + body), `ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(user)` (201 + Location header), `ResponseEntity.notFound().build()` (404 + no body), `ResponseEntity.status(422).body(errorDetails)`. Use when you need fine-grained HTTP response control; use `@ResponseStatus` for simple fixed-status methods.

questions.question: What is `@ExceptionHandler` and `@ControllerAdvice` in Spring?

options.text: @ExceptionHandler suppresses exceptions so they don't reach the client

@ExceptionHandler maps specific exceptions to HTTP responses in a controller. @ControllerAdvice applies exception handling globally across all controllers — used to build a consistent error response format
@ControllerAdvice is for AOP; @ExceptionHandler is for validation
They are only available in Spring Boot, not plain Spring MVC

questions.explanation: `@ExceptionHandler(UserNotFoundException.class)` in a controller handles that exception for that controller only. `@RestControllerAdvice` (= `@ControllerAdvice` + `@ResponseBody`) handles exceptions globally. Best practice: one `@RestControllerAdvice` class with handlers for all exceptions, returning a consistent error DTO with status, message, timestamp, and traceId.

questions.question: What is `@Valid` and bean validation in Spring?

options.text: @Valid triggers Spring to run the method and validate its result

@Valid on a method parameter triggers JSR-380 (Bean Validation) — annotations like @NotNull, @Size, @Email on the parameter's class fields are validated; ConstraintViolationException / MethodArgumentNotValidException on failure
@Valid marks a class as a Spring-managed bean
@Valid only works with String fields

questions.explanation: Spring integrates with Hibernate Validator (JSR-380). Annotate DTO fields: `@NotNull`, `@NotBlank`, `@Size(min=1, max=50)`, `@Email`, `@Pattern`, `@Min`, `@Max`, `@Valid` (for nested objects). In controllers, `@Valid @RequestBody CreateUserRequest req` triggers validation. On failure: `MethodArgumentNotValidException` — handle in `@ExceptionHandler` to return 400 with field errors.

questions.question: What is Spring WebFlux and when would you use it over Spring MVC?

options.text: WebFlux is the same as Spring MVC — just a different name

WebFlux is Spring's reactive web framework built on Project Reactor — use for high-concurrency I/O-bound services where you need non-blocking I/O and back-pressure, avoiding thread-per-request blocking
WebFlux is only for streaming video content
WebFlux uses more threads than Spring MVC for better performance

questions.explanation: Spring MVC: blocking I/O, thread-per-request (Servlet). Spring WebFlux: non-blocking I/O, event-loop model (Netty by default). Uses `Mono<T>` (0-1 result) and `Flux<T>` (0-N results). Benefits: handles more concurrent requests with fewer threads for I/O-bound work. Drawbacks: harder to reason about, reactive library must be used throughout the stack. MVC is simpler and usually sufficient — choose WebFlux for very high concurrency requirements.

questions.question: What is the Spring `@Async` annotation and how does it work?

options.text: @Async makes the annotated method synchronous — blocking the caller until done
@Async causes the method to execute in a separate thread from the caller's thread pool — the caller returns immediately, getting a Future/CompletableFuture for the result
@Async is only for @Scheduled methods
@Async automatically handles transactions from the calling thread

questions.explanation: Enable with `@EnableAsync` on a config class. Method must be `public` and called from OUTSIDE the class (self-invocation bypasses proxy). Returns `void`, `Future<T>`, or `CompletableFuture<T>`. Spring runs it on a configured `TaskExecutor`. Without custom config, uses a `SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor` (creates new thread per call — configure `ThreadPoolTaskExecutor` in production). Exceptions in void @Async methods go to `AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler`.

questions.question: What is `@Cacheable` in Spring?

options.text: @Cacheable makes a method result available globally as a static variable

@Cacheable caches method return values — on subsequent calls with the same parameters, the cached value is returned without executing the method. Spring abstracts over multiple cache providers (Caffeine, Redis, EhCache)
@Cacheable is only for database query results
@Cacheable stores values in the Spring application context

questions.explanation: Enable with `@EnableCaching`. `@Cacheable("users")` caches by all parameters by default; `key="#id"` specifies the cache key. `@CacheEvict("users")` clears entries. `@CachePut` always executes and updates cache. Configure a `CacheManager` bean for the provider (Caffeine for in-memory, Redis for distributed). Spring abstracts the cache — swap providers without changing code.

questions.question: What is `@Scheduled` in Spring Boot?

options.text: @Scheduled starts an HTTP server for scheduled HTTP callbacks
@Scheduled runs a method on a fixed schedule — using fixedRate, fixedDelay, or cron expressions. Requires @EnableScheduling
@Scheduled is the same as @Async
@Scheduled can only be used in @Controller classes

questions.explanation: Enable with `@EnableScheduling`. `@Scheduled(fixedRate = 5000)`: runs every 5 seconds (next execution starts 5s after last START). `@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 5000)`: 5 seconds after last COMPLETION. `@Scheduled(cron = "0 0 2 * * ?")`: standard cron expression (daily at 2am). By default runs on a single-threaded executor — configure `TaskScheduler` bean for thread pool. Long-running tasks block the scheduler.

questions.question: What is the difference between `@SpringBootTest` and `@WebMvcTest` for testing?

options.text: @SpringBootTest is for unit tests; @WebMvcTest is for integration tests
@SpringBootTest loads the full ApplicationContext (integration test); @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer (controllers, filters, converters) with mocked services — faster and more focused
@WebMvcTest requires a running server; @SpringBootTest does not
They are identical — only the annotation name differs

questions.explanation: `@SpringBootTest`: full context, can test whole application including database. `@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)`: only loads web layer, `@Service`/`@Repository` beans must be `@MockBean`'d. Use `MockMvc` to simulate HTTP requests without starting a real server. `@DataJpaTest`: JPA layer only with in-memory H2. `@MockBean`: replaces a bean in context with a Mockito mock.

questions.question: What are Spring Profiles and how do you use them?

options.text: Spring Profiles are performance profiling tools built into Spring
Profiles allow different configurations for different environments (dev, test, prod). Beans can be activated per profile with @Profile; activate with spring.profiles.active property
Profiles are only for database configuration
Profiles replace environment variables in Spring Boot

questions.explanation: `@Profile("dev")` on a `@Bean` or `@Configuration` class: only active when dev profile is active. Activate: `spring.profiles.active=prod` in `application.properties`, `-Dspring.profiles.active=prod` JVM arg, or `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` env var. Profile-specific files: `application-dev.yml` auto-loaded when dev profile is active. Use for environment-specific beans (H2 vs PostgreSQL DataSource, mock vs real services).

questions.question: What is transaction propagation in Spring and what are the main propagation types?

options.text: Transaction propagation determines which database is used

Propagation controls how transactions behave when methods call each other: REQUIRED (join or create), REQUIRES_NEW (always new, suspends current), SUPPORTS (join if exists, else none), MANDATORY (must have existing), NEVER (must not have existing), NOT_SUPPORTED (always non-transactional)
All Spring methods share one transaction — propagation is automatic
Propagation only applies to read-only transactions

questions.explanation: Key propagation types: `REQUIRED` (default): joins existing transaction; creates new if none. `REQUIRES_NEW`: always starts new transaction, suspends current — useful for audit logging that must commit even if caller rolls back. `SUPPORTS`: transactional if caller is, non-transactional otherwise. `NOT_SUPPORTED`: always non-transactional (suspends current). `MANDATORY`: must have existing transaction — throws if none. `NEVER`: must NOT have transaction.

questions.question: What is the difference between constructor injection and field injection in Spring?

options.text: Field injection is required for immutable dependencies; constructor injection is not supported
Constructor injection makes required dependencies explicit, supports final fields, and improves testability; field injection hides dependencies and is harder to test directly
They behave identically and have the same testability characteristics
Constructor injection requires every dependency to be a prototype bean

questions.explanation: Constructor injection declares required dependencies in the constructor, making them explicit and allowing fields to be final. It supports straightforward unit testing without a Spring container and helps prevent partially initialized objects. Field injection relies on reflection and hides dependencies; constructor injection is generally preferred for required collaborators.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Spring Filter and a HandlerInterceptor?

options.text: A Filter runs within the Servlet container chain and can act before Spring MVC; a HandlerInterceptor runs within Spring MVC around handler execution
An interceptor runs before the Servlet container; a filter runs only after the controller
They are identical and configured in the same way
A Filter can only inspect response bodies, while an interceptor can only inspect request headers

questions.explanation: A Servlet Filter is part of the servlet filter chain and can process requests before they reach the DispatcherServlet, as well as responses on the way back. A Spring MVC HandlerInterceptor operates within the MVC request handling lifecycle, with callbacks such as preHandle, postHandle, and afterCompletion. Filters are commonly used for cross-cutting servlet concerns; interceptors are useful for handler-aware MVC concerns.

questions.question: What is the N+1 query problem in Spring Data JPA/Hibernate?

options.text: It occurs when one query is executed for every database table
It occurs when loading a set of entities triggers one initial query plus additional queries for related entities, potentially causing many database round trips
It means a transaction retries a failed query N+1 times
It is a database connection pool configuration error

questions.explanation: The N+1 problem commonly occurs when an initial query loads N parent entities and accessing a lazy relationship triggers an additional query for each parent. This can create many database round trips. Possible remedies include fetch joins, entity graphs, DTO projections, or batch fetching, chosen according to the use case and pagination requirements.

questions.question: Why might `@Transactional` not work when one method calls another method in the same Spring bean?

options.text: Spring transactions only work with private constructors
Proxy-based transaction management is typically bypassed by self-invocation because the call does not pass through the Spring proxy
Transactions cannot be used with public methods
Spring disables transactions when methods return void

questions.explanation: In the common proxy-based transaction model, Spring applies transactional behavior when a call enters through the proxy. A method calling another method on `this` bypasses that proxy, so the inner method's transactional metadata may not be applied as expected. Common solutions include moving the transactional method to another bean or redesigning the boundary; AspectJ weaving is another option.

questions.question: What is the difference between `@SpringBootTest` and `@WebMvcTest`?

options.text: `@SpringBootTest` loads an application context for broader integration testing; `@WebMvcTest` focuses on the MVC layer and typically uses mocked collaborators
`@WebMvcTest` starts a full production database and all application services
`@SpringBootTest` can test only controllers
They are aliases for the same test annotation

questions.explanation: `@SpringBootTest` creates an application context using Spring Boot's test support and is suitable for broader integration tests. `@WebMvcTest` loads a focused MVC test slice, typically including controller and MVC infrastructure while excluding most application components; dependencies are commonly supplied as mocks. Use the narrowest test slice that verifies the behavior you need.

questions.question: What is a Stream in Java and how does it differ from a Collection?

options.text: A Stream is a sequence of elements supporting sequential and parallel aggregate operations; unlike Collections it does not store data
A Stream is a data structure that stores elements in memory like a List
A Stream is a byte-level I/O abstraction for reading files
A Stream is a thread-safe collection for concurrent access

questions.explanation: A Stream is not a data structure — it carries elements from a source (Collection, array, I/O channel) through a pipeline of operations. Collections store data; Streams process data. A Stream can only be consumed once and does not modify its source.

questions.question: What is the difference between intermediate and terminal stream operations?

options.text: Intermediate operations return a Stream and are lazy; terminal operations return a result or side-effect and trigger pipeline execution
Intermediate operations execute immediately; terminal operations are deferred
Intermediate operations can only filter; terminal operations can only collect
There is no functional difference — both execute the same way

questions.explanation: Intermediate operations (filter, map, sorted, distinct, limit, skip, flatMap, peek) are lazy — they build up the pipeline but do not execute until a terminal operation (collect, forEach, reduce, count, findFirst, anyMatch, toList) is called. This enables optimization such as short-circuit evaluation.

questions.question: What does `map()` do in a Stream pipeline?

options.text: Transforms each element to another value using a Function, producing a new Stream of the transformed values
Filters elements based on a predicate
Flattens nested collections into a single stream
Collects elements into a Map

questions.explanation: `map(Function<T,R>)` applies the function to each element and returns a `Stream<R>`. For primitive specializations use `mapToInt`, `mapToLong`, `mapToDouble`. It is a 1-to-1 transformation, unlike `flatMap` which is 1-to-many.

questions.question: What is the difference between `map()` and `flatMap()` in Stream?

options.text: `map()` is one-to-one; `flatMap()` maps each element to a Stream and then flattens all those streams into one
`flatMap()` is faster than `map()` for large collections
`map()` works on primitives; `flatMap()` works on objects
`flatMap()` filters null values automatically while `map()` does not

questions.explanation: `flatMap(Function<T, Stream<R>>)` is useful when each element maps to zero, one, or many results. Example: `Stream<List<String>>` → `flatMap(Collection::stream)` → `Stream<String>`. Without `flatMap` you would get `Stream<Stream<String>>`.

questions.question: What is a functional interface in Java?

options.text: An interface with exactly one abstract method, which can be used as the target of a lambda expression or method reference
An interface that extends java.util.function.Function
Any interface annotated with @FunctionalInterface regardless of method count
An interface with only default and static methods

questions.explanation: A functional interface has exactly one abstract method (SAM — Single Abstract Method). It may have default and static methods. The `@FunctionalInterface` annotation is optional but documents the intent and causes a compile error if the contract is violated. Key examples: `Runnable`, `Callable`, `Comparator`, `Function`, `Predicate`, `Consumer`, `Supplier`.

questions.question: What are the core functional interfaces in `java.util.function` and what do they represent?

options.text: Function<T,R> (T→R), Predicate<T> (T→boolean), Consumer<T> (T→void), Supplier<T> (→T), UnaryOperator<T> (T→T), BinaryOperator<T> (T,T→T)
Function<T,R>, Iterator<T>, Comparator<T>, Runnable, Callable<T>
Mapper<T,R>, Filter<T>, Reducer<T>, Collector<T>
Observable<T>, Publisher<T>, Subscriber<T>, Processor<T>

questions.explanation: The core `java.util.function` interfaces: `Function<T,R>` transforms T to R; `Predicate<T>` tests a condition; `Consumer<T>` consumes T with no return; `Supplier<T>` produces T with no input; `UnaryOperator<T>` is Function<T,T>; `BinaryOperator<T>` is BiFunction<T,T,T>. Bi-variants exist for two-argument forms.

questions.question: What is a lambda expression in Java?

options.text: A concise anonymous function that can be used wherever a functional interface is expected, with syntax (params) -> body
A named inner class that implements a functional interface
A special type of method that can be passed as an argument to any method
An annotation that marks a method as functional

questions.explanation: Lambda expressions provide a shorthand for implementing functional interfaces. Syntax: `(parameters) -> expression` or `(parameters) -> { statements; }`. They close over effectively-final variables from the enclosing scope. Under the hood, lambdas use `invokedynamic` and are NOT anonymous inner classes.

questions.question: What are method references and what are the four kinds?

options.text: Shorthand for lambdas that just delegate to an existing method: static (Class::staticMethod), instance on a particular instance (obj::method), instance on an arbitrary instance (Class::instanceMethod), constructor (Class::new)
References to methods stored in variables, similar to function pointers in C
Annotations that point to a method implementation for documentation
Only two kinds exist: static method references and constructor references

questions.explanation: The four method reference kinds: (1) Static: `Integer::parseInt`; (2) Bound instance: `str::toUpperCase` (specific object); (3) Unbound instance: `String::toUpperCase` (first arg is the receiver); (4) Constructor: `ArrayList::new`. They are equivalent to a lambda that only calls that method.

questions.question: What is `Optional<T>` and why was it introduced?

options.text: A container that may or may not hold a non-null value, introduced to express the absence of a value explicitly and reduce NullPointerExceptions
A special nullable type that automatically handles null without throwing exceptions
A thread-safe wrapper around a nullable value for concurrent use
A replacement for the `null` keyword that was deprecated in Java 8

questions.explanation: `Optional<T>` forces callers to explicitly handle the empty case. Created via `Optional.of(value)`, `Optional.ofNullable(value)`, or `Optional.empty()`. Key methods: `isPresent()`, `get()`, `orElse()`, `orElseGet()`, `orElseThrow()`, `map()`, `flatMap()`, `filter()`, `ifPresent()`. Should be used as a return type, not as field type or parameter type.

questions.question: What is the difference between `Optional.orElse()` and `Optional.orElseGet()`?

options.text: `orElse(value)` always evaluates the argument eagerly; `orElseGet(Supplier)` lazily evaluates only if the Optional is empty
`orElseGet()` throws if the Optional is empty; `orElse()` returns null
They are identical; `orElseGet` is just a more verbose form of `orElse`
